Why is it important?

Music is a form of personal and cultural expression and a way of connecting through sound and silence. Music has occupied a significant place in cultures around the world and across times. Learning in music stimulates students’ curiosity and creativity, and enables personal expression through sound. Performing, listening and composing music contributes to cognitive development, memory and wellbeing.

Developing aural awareness is foundational to music education, and listening is integral to all musical experiences. Listening skills include the ability to focus on, hear, understand and respond to musical stimuli and discriminate between sounds. For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, listening may include the use of assistive technology, or accessing music through touch or sight.

In Stage 1, it is important for students to explore ways musical ideas are communicated through sound. Students develop greater musical awareness by engaging – through performing, listening and composing – with a wide musical repertoire from historical periods and cultural contexts around the world.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Music provides a rich platform on which to build a musical vocabulary and language comprehension. The elements of music are a good starting point for explicitly teaching vocabulary in the context of music.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require specific and targeted teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers focus on the following aspects of the elements of music in Stage 1.

Element of musicKey questionsVocabulary examples
Duration

The lengths of sounds and silences in music.		Is this sound longer or shorter than the next sound?Tempo, beat and rhythm patterns, rests.
Pitch

The relative highness or lowness of sounds.		Is this sound higher, lower or at the same pitch as the other sound?Pitch, melody, melodic pattern, melodic shape.
Performing media

The instruments/voices/sound sources used in a piece of music.		What instruments or sound sources are being played in this music?Sound source, voice, percussion, wood/wind/skin/string instrument, environmental sounds.
Timbre

The distinctive quality of a sound.		How would you describe the sounds being made?Rich, bright, warm, smooth.
Dynamics

The volume of sound.		When did the music change to become louder or softer?Dynamics, getting louder, getting softer.
Expression

The musical detail that articulates a style or interpretation of a style.		How did the changes in volume affect the mood of the music?Expression, mood.
Structure

The design or form in music. It refers to how a composition is constructed in sections or parts.		How did the music change from the verse to the chorus?Structure, sections A and B, verse and chorus.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Understanding and using grammar when interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Stage 1 content provides students with opportunities to develop an understanding of diverse sounds and instruments used in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander music. Students gain an understanding of music as an important Cultural Practice.

Performing: Music is performed to communicate musical ideas through sound

Students perform music by singing, moving and playing repertoire or original musical ideas. They may use voice, body percussion, sound sources, instruments and/or digital technologies to play, improvise, organise, manipulate and record sounds. It is important to set up classroom expectations about the care and use of instruments, and to establish routines for when to play instruments and when to hold them still. Arranging students in a semicircle can assist them to follow visual cues and gestures when performing.

Singing is foundational to learning in music. Voice is a personal instrument that is a means of expression. As music is an aural art form, the interaction between voice and the ear, through singing and speech, is important for musical development. Explicitly teach students to sing simple songs and rhymes, and to chant, within a small pitch range. Students may need to practise the pronunciation and articulation of some words. When teaching rhymes and chants, provide opportunities for students to predict and fill in the missing rhyming words. Encourage students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing to feel their throat or diaphragm when they sing so they can feel the vibration. Use instruments that produce clean sounds when accompanying a singer, and explore digital colour coding to highlight the lyrics when singing.

When students play tuned and untuned instruments they may echo or copy short rhythm patterns, which reinforces understanding of the elements of music.

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs for peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups for the wider school community.

Listening: Musical ideas are conveyed through sound

It is important to set up expectations for listening behaviours in the class. Listening is integrated in all aspects of learning in music and is fundamental to all performing and composing activities. Students experience music and develop aural awareness using listening skills to consider ways the elements of music are used and to describe sounds using musical vocabulary.

Using body movements to express musical ideas is important for listening. Encourage students to use body movements, march to a beat or respond to a melody. Using props or actions to direct listening can support students to recognise when the music changes; for example, moving ribbons or elastics up and down to show the shape of a melody, or passing a ball to the beat, nodding heads for verse, and tapping toes for chorus. Teachers may support students by asking:

  • How did the music change?
  • What are the sections in this music?
  • Do you notice any repeated patterns in this music?
  • How would you describe the overall mood or atmosphere of this music?

Symbols and graphic notation are a way to represent sounds in music. It is important for students to connect sound to physical or printed symbols. Starting with simple symbols or stick notation builds understanding and lays the foundation for more complex notation as students develop as musicians. Some students may need to be supported to learn about symbols or graphic notation through the use of multisensory tools or props; for example, cups and pop sticks.

Image long description: An example of graphic notation with a stick to represent a whole note, 2 sticks joined at the top to represent 2 half notes, followed by a stick to represent a whole note; for example, taa ti-ti taa.

In Stage 1, HSIE students learn how People use stories, images, objects and sites to understand the ancient past. Teachers may like to deepen students’ understanding of music in historical contexts, including ancient music practices, to recognise how music is influenced by time and place.

Composing: Music is composed to communicate musical ideas through sound

Composing focuses on organising sounds to create music through singing, moving and playing original musical ideas.

Students explore ways to imitate and vary patterns and organise sounds into simple structures. They are encouraged to experiment, change, improvise, share and graphically notate new musical ideas in cooperation with others. Teachers can model ways to compose music with students and support them to experiment with:

  • ways to vary speech chants
  • various stimuli to make music
  • ways to use voice to imitate animals or other sounds
  • creating movements or body percussion to accompany songs
  • creating and using symbols or graphic notation to represent musical ideas.

Image long description: An example of graphic notation using symbols to represent sounds. From left to right, the symbols are 2 wave symbols, 2 apple symbols, a zigzag symbol, 2 wave symbols, 2 apple symbols.

Vocabulary:  blow, compose, echo, gesture, graphic notation, hum, instrumental music, modify, musician, perform, pluck, round, speed, strike, voice, vocal music, whisper, strum, symbol.

Making connections through related content

Mathematics:

  • Forming groups A: Count in multiples using rhythmic and skip counting; Use skip counting patterns; Model and use equal groups of objects to represent multiplication; Recognise and represent division
  • Representing whole numbers A: Use counting sequences of ones with two-digit numbers and beyond; Continue and create number patterns

HSIE:

  • People learn about the past by engaging with stories, images, objects and sites: People use stories, images, objects and sites to understand the ancient past

Why is it important?

Visual arts have provided a means of communication, creative expression and representation in cultures around the world and throughout history. Learning in Visual Arts develops students’ understanding of the relationships between artists, artworks, the world and audiences. In Visual Arts students explore the ways materials, techniques and processes are used to represent subject matter and ideas in artworks.

In Stage 1, students make artworks connected to their experiences and understanding of the world. They begin to realise that subject matter and ideas can be represented in different ways through art forms. Students understand artworks can be experienced and described in various ways and that they can form opinions about artworks. They recognise that artworks communicate ideas to audiences when shared through displays and exhibitions.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language of visual arts, including the vocabulary of the elements of art and design, provides the foundations for learning. Students develop the vocabulary necessary to reflect on their own artmaking experiences and to describe artworks from a range of contexts.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions related to artworks they are making or appreciating. See the table below for examples.

ConceptsKey questionsVocabulary examples
ArtistWhat ideas do you have for your artwork?

What techniques has the artist used to make this artwork and what effect do they have?		2D art form, 3D art form, object, sculpture, techniques, tools.
ArtworkWhat sorts of colours have you used in your artwork and why did you choose them?

What materials do you think have been used to make this artwork?		Asymmetrical, ceramic, clay, ochre, pattern, primary colour, secondary colour, shade, surface, symmetrical, tint.
WorldHow have you represented ideas or subject matter about the world in your artwork?

What do you think the artist was thinking about when they made this artwork?		Culture, purpose, subject matter, symbol.
AudienceHow would you like to display your artwork?

Where is this artwork exhibited and who do you think will be able to visit it?		Exhibit, frame, mount.

The following English content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes:

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities 

Stage 1 content provides students with opportunities to develop an understanding of how to interpret Cultural Knowledges and meaning in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander artworks. 

Making: Artists use materials and techniques to represent subject matter and ideas in artworks

Subject matter and ideas for art making may develop from students’ own experiences of the world or may connect to learning in art appreciation or other learning areas. It is important for students to have opportunities to choose how to represent subject matter and ideas based on their own interpretations of the world.

Students recognise that artworks can be made in various ways such as:

  • realistic ways: representing an urban, rural or remote Australian place by conveying features of a selected landscape
  • imaginative ways: representing characters or imaginary creatures from stories or other worlds
  • expressive ways: representing features of the sky during the day or night using their knowledge of colour, colour mixing, tints, shades and expressive mark-making techniques.

It is important for students to continue mixing colours to make tints and shades. Using paint or digital technologies, students explore ways to create and use a selection of tones to express ideas and produce effects in artworks.

Students make 3D sculptural forms using modelling and construction materials. When working with malleable materials, it is important for students to use hand-building techniques and simple tools. Students may decorate the surface of a clay form by carving marks, textures or designs into the surface. For example, students may engrave patterns or images inspired by ancient vases or vessels to connect with learning in art appreciation.

Some students may require adjustments to make artworks, including those with low vision or who are blind. This could include using materials with tactile qualities, providing audio transcripts describing an artwork to help them understand things they may never have seen or experienced, or adding scents and textures to materials for modelling.

Appreciating: Artists represent subject matter and ideas in artworks which can be experienced and described by audiences

Students observe artworks from contexts around the world and communicate ideas about ways artists represent subject matter and ideas in artworks to audiences. They observe the materials and techniques used to make artworks and the qualities within artworks. Students use the vocabulary of the elements of art and design to discuss ideas, feelings and opinions about artworks.

Students may explore ancient or historical artworks to connect to learning in HSIE, for example, students may investigate ancient vessels, such as these.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions such as:

  • What patterns, images or symbols do you observe on the vessel?
  • What do you think the images or symbols are about?
  • What materials do you think were used to make this container?
  • What do these containers tell you about the ancient past?
  • How might this artwork influence your own art making?

Students investigate artworks from cultural contexts around the world, such as Kenyan beadwork.

Credit: www.storyboardthat.com

Students respond to questions such as:

  • What do you think this jewellery is made from?
  • What do you notice about the colours of the beads?
  • Do you think the colours symbolise anything?
  • How would you describe the patterns created with the beads?
  • Why have these artworks been created and how are they connected to a place?

Students can be supported to experience and describe ideas in artworks by scaffolding questions and encouraging further clarification in their answers by redirecting, probing or reinforcing responses.

Exhibiting: Artworks can be displayed and exhibited for audiences to experience

Students begin to realise that artworks are displayed and exhibited for audiences to experience when they display their own artworks at school. Students may consider ways to display and exhibit their artworks according to the type of artwork and the audience.

Students may consider the location in which their artworks will be displayed and think about, for example, ways to work with the positive and negative spaces on the wall. Students may attach a title, short description or story to accompany their artwork in a display. They may explain the materials, techniques, artmaking process or how and why they made particular choices in their art making; for example, ‘I chose to use … because …’

Students can be supported to recognise the organisation of the artworks on display by providing a model example using visual, tactile, audio or written representations.

Vocabulary: 2D art form, 3D art form, acrylic paint, adjoining, asymmetry, clay, colour, culture, diagonal, display, frame, hand-building, hard, horizontal, ink, line, materials, mount, natural pigments, negative, space, objects, ochre, overlapping, pattern, positive space, repeating, rough, sculpture, shade, smooth, soft, subject matter, surface, symbols, symmetry, techniques, tertiary colours, texture, tint, tone, vertical.

Making connections through related content

Human Society and its Environment:

  • People are connected to places and groups: People show their connection to places using geographical information
  • People learn about the past by engaging with stories, images, objects and sites: People use stories, images, objects and sites to understand the ancient past

Mathematics:

  • Two-dimensional spatial structure A: 2D shapes: Transform shapes with slides and reflections
  • Two-dimensional spatial structure B: 2D shapes: Represent, combine and separate two-dimensional shapes
  • Three-dimensional spatial structure A: 3D objects: Recognise familiar three-dimensional objects
  • Three-dimensional spatial structure B: 3D objects: Describe the features of three-dimensional objects

Why is it important?

Dance is a distinct form of movement that is universal to the human experience. Throughout time, dance has brought people together to share knowledge, culture and ideas. In dance, students use the body as an instrument to express and communicate ideas.

In Stage 2, it is important for students to connect shapes and movements into sequences to communicate ideas to audiences. They use their oral and written language skills to describe how the elements of dance are used to communicate intent.

As a movement-based artform, dance is beneficial to motor development, strength, and physical and emotional wellbeing. All bodies are diverse and move in different ways. Some students with physical disability may require adjustments, including assistive devices such as walkers or wheelchairs. Adjustments can be made to the environment, equipment and instructions to create an inclusive learning environment.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language and vocabulary of the elements of dance – space, time and dynamics – helps students understand and describe dance as they learn to compose, perform and appreciate it.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following elements of dance in Stage 2.

Element of danceKey questionsVocabulary examples
Space
The components of space, including shape, level, direction, dimension, pathways, floor patterns and stage space.		How can you change the pathway of your movements to express your ideas?

How did the dancers use the stage space during the performance?		Shape: symmetrical, asymmetrical, geometric, angular, curved.

Level: low, middle, high.

Direction: horizontal, vertical.

Pathway: curved, zigzag.
Time
The components of time, including metre, rhythm, accent, tempo, duration and stillness.		How can you vary the speed of your movements and incorporate stillness into your dance?

How did the performers respond to tempo and rhythm changes in the music during the dance?		Slow, medium, fast, accelerating, decelerating tempo.
Dynamics
The release of energy, weight and/or force over a period of time to create movement qualities.		How can you change the quality of your movements to create contrasting effects by adding greater or less force?

How did the dancers use dynamics to express ideas in the performance?		Soft, hard, smooth, sharp.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

In Stage 2, students explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Cultural Knowledges are expressed through dance. Students are introduced to the importance of protocols when engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dances.

Composing: Dance is composed using the elements of dance to communicate ideas

Students explore ways to communicate ideas to audiences through dance. They further develop skills in sequencing movements by responding to stimuli, collaborating with others, and using repeating and contrasting patterns of movement. They also apply communication and cooperation skills when working with peers.

Students improvise and modify ways to use the elements of dance to make shapes and movements and communicate ideas. For example, students can explore space by changing the pathway of movement to include straight, curved or zigzag sequences. They may explore the impact of time by varying movements in response to rhythm and tempo changes in music. Creating contrasting effects with highly energetic or low and slow movements supports students in exploring the effects of dynamics.

As students collaborate with others to compose a group-devised dance sequence, they may focus on:

  • refining dance shapes and movements
  • inserting small breaks of stillness
  • using patterns of movement to transition between sections of the dance
  • repeating or adding contrasting actions to reflect changes in the music
  • rearranging movements within a sequence by altering, swapping, repeating or reversing actions.

Students can use notes and annotations to document and plan the process. These may take the form of:

  • mind maps to illustrate themes and ideas and to highlight connections
  • timelines to outline the sequence of movements in a performance
  • stage plans to indicate the position of dancers in the space at the beginning, middle and end of a sequence.

Teachers play an important role in ensuring students develop safe dance practices by engaging in warm-up and cool-down exercises, and following protocols.

Performing: Dance is performed to communicate ideas to audiences

Providing time to rehearse movements and dance sequences supports students to enhance their dance technique. Students make adjustments to body alignment, control and balance through focused practice and by responding to peer and teacher feedback.

Sharing the progress of dance compositions or a dance performance provides rich opportunities for students to apply their growing understanding of how the elements of dance communicate ideas. Students may perform during the process of composing and once a composition is complete.

Making digital recordings of a dance while composing or performing provides students with opportunities to reflect on and discuss parts of a dance that communicate ideas well and areas that may be strengthened. School policies should be followed when making or sharing recordings of students.

Appreciating: The elements of dance are used in various ways to convey ideas through movement

Students develop a growing understanding of the elements of dance and how ideas are conveyed through dance in various ways, in cultural and historical contexts around the world. They extend their oral and written language skills by describing how the elements of dance are used to communicate intent. Students may draw from their own experiences to connect with different dance works.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions such as:

  • What are the distinct features of the dance? (For example, groupings or spatial relationships between performers; dancers moving in unison or separately.)
  • What objects are used in the dance, and do they have cultural significance? (For example, objects or props used to tell a story.)
  • When and where is this dance performed, and what is its historical significance? (For example, traditional or cultural dances.)

Vocabulary: accelerating, asymmetrical, contrasting, curved, decelerating, horizontal, pathways, protocols, rhythm, stimulus, symmetrical, tempo, vertical, zigzag.

Making connections through related content

PDHPE:

  • Movement skill and physical activity
  • Self-management and interpersonal skills

content.value:
Why is it important?

Drama is a practice of embodied storytelling and a form of communication in cultures around the world. Humans have an innate desire to explore the way people interact with one another and the world. Drama experiences widen students’ understandings of people and relationships as they explore situations from different perspectives. Students develop empathy as they experience what it feels like to ‘walk in someone else’s shoes’.

In Stage 2, it is important for students to devise dramatic situations by collaborating with others. Students explore ways to indicate time and build dramatic tension and atmosphere to further enrich their performances. By exploring dramatic practices from cultural and historical contexts around the world, they widen their world view and develop deeper understandings of people, time and place.

Some students with disability may need adjustments to access and participate in dramatic experiences. This could include adjustments to support movement, communication, access to the drama space, sensory experiences and collaboration with others.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language and vocabulary of the dramatic elements provides the foundations for learning in the context of drama.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following dramatic elements in Stage 2.

Dramatic elementFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Role

Points of view, objects or personas presented through embodiment.		How did you make changes to your role during the rehearsals?

How did the actors show the relationship between their roles in the drama?		Performer, relationships.
Character

A dramatic role built with complexity, personality and/or background.		How will you show changes in your character’s feelings and attitudes?

If you could provide feedback to the performer playing that character, what would it be?		Personality, feelings, attitude.
Tension

The energy that drives drama. Tension can be developed through embodiment, structure, problems, tasks, conflict and manipulation of audience expectations.		What points of conflict could you develop in this drama?

How did the characters create a sense of tension in the performance?		Goal, task, tension, conflict, surprise.
Situation

The circumstances that characters experience and that shape their actions and intentions.		How can you use objects, props or costumes to help establish the situation?

What questions would you ask the characters to find out more about the situation?		Belief, fiction.
Space

The shape and spatial design of the performance area, and the spatial dynamics and relationships between performers, performance area and audience.		How will you use the space to establish a setting?

How was the performance space used to create belief in the drama?		Entry, exit, position.
Time

The transformation of the real time of the audience to the imagined time of the performance.		How can you indicate the time of day in your drama?

How did the actors move backwards and forwards in time in the drama?		Fast motion, slow motion.
Structure

The way a dramatic work is shaped, which can include cause and effect, narrative, plot, and sequencing of images, motifs or ideas.		How could the narrative of your drama change if it were told from the perspective of another character?

How does this style of drama vary from those in other traditions around the world?		Beginning, middle, end.
Language

Ways of expressing and receiving images, ideas, feelings and stories, using spoken, visual, written and/or gestural communication strategies.		How can you adapt the pace, pitch or tone of your voice to suit the character?

How did the actors use language to create tension in this scene?		Spoken language, written language; pace, pitch, tone of voice.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words
  • Understanding and responding to literature: Characterisation

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in this focus area provides students with opportunities to consider the preparations and practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander performers. Students gain insight into how Cultural information is communicated through dramatic works.

Making: Drama is made using the dramatic elements to shape ideas and stories

It is important for students to experience a wide selection of drama forms and styles. Students develop imagination, creativity and confidence as they enact ideas using improvisation, still image and mime. Teachers can support students in planning and developing a script for a drama enacted through storytelling, readers’ theatre or devised drama.

Teachers can provide sources such as objects, props, sounds, texts, themes, natural materials or images to support students in devising dramatic situations. Consider appropriate stimuli to suit students’ needs, such as visual or tactile objects for students with hearing impairment.

As students gain deeper understandings of characters, they may experiment with ways to demonstrate characters’ feelings, values and attitudes by adapting elements of voice or language:

  • pace: slow for tiredness, fast for excitement or pausing for confusion
  • pitch: low for a giant or high for a child
  • tone: disappointed to express sadness, or excited to express joy.

Some EAL/D students in the early phases of English language learning may be developing their understanding of prosodic features of oral language and may need explicit teaching to make connections between pace, pitch, tone and meaning.

Developing tension in a drama assists in shaping the story to make it more interesting and intriguing for the audience. Students may investigate ways to build tension through:

  • a situation (for example, characters solving a challenging problem)
  • time (for example, characters running late for an event)
  • relationships (for example, characters having a disagreement)
  • surprise (for example, characters meeting someone unexpectedly)
  • mystery (for example, characters trying to find a missing pet).

When learning about characters and storytelling in Drama, teachers may make connections to Narrative and Characterisation in Stage 2 of the English syllabus.

It is important for students to engage in safe drama practices by de-roling and stepping out of character after a drama experience. Creating routines using physical movements such as shaking out the arms and legs, removing costumes and props, and taking time to reflect on experiences can assist students in stepping out of character.

Performing: Drama is performed to embody and enact characters, ideas and stories for audiences

Devising and performing drama relies on students’ ability to collaborate, cooperate and compromise effectively. Teachers may assist with prompts such as:

  • How can we ensure that each member of the group’s ideas are heard and considered?
  • How can we compromise (meet in the middle) when devising ideas?

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs to peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups to the wider school community.

It is important for students to reflect on their own drama-making experiences and performances to consider ways to refine or improve their drama skills. Students reflect on and discuss the effects created by selecting elements of drama to communicate ideas. Teachers may assist with prompts such as:

  • If you were to perform your drama again, what is something you could do differently?
  • How did you use pitch, pace and tone of voice or language to express how your character was feeling?

Appreciating: The dramatic elements are used to shape meaning for audiences

As students explore drama from cultural and historical contexts around the world, they begin to understand how dramatic practitioners use dramatic elements to shape meaning according to context. They may explore traditions in drama forms or styles, such as comparing puppetry practices from various times and places, such as the Indonesian Wayang kulit, the Italian tradition of Pinocchio and the Salzburg Marionette Theatre.

Credit: PLAINVIEW/iStock
Image long description: Javanese shadow puppet made from buffalo hide used in Wayang kulit shadow puppet plays. The puppet has exaggerated features and a thin, spindly build, and is depicted wearing ornate traditional clothing and jewellery.

Credit: Serts/iStock
Image long description: A wooden Pinocchio puppet from Italy, suspended from a rope. The puppet resembles a boy wearing a red jacket and hat, and is made of simple wooden shapes and bold colours.

Credit: Universal Images Group North America LLC/DeAgostini/Alamy Stock Photo
Image long description: A marionette puppet of a man wearing a powdered wig (peruke) from the Salzburg Theatre, Vienna. It is costumed in traditional European Enlightenment-era clothing.

Students can investigate the types of materials used to make the puppets and their manipulation techniques, as well as the cultural stories and ideas expressed in the performances.

Students begin to make connections between drama they have experienced and their own personal, social and cultural contexts, gathering ideas to support their own drama-making and performing experiences.

Vocabulary: attitudes, belief, conflict, fast motion, fiction, gesture, improvisation, pace, performer, personality, pitch, relationships, slow motion, stage geography, status, stimuli, surprise, tension, tone, transition.

Why is it important?

Music is a form of personal and cultural expression and a way of connecting through sound and silence. Music has occupied a significant place in cultures around the world and across times. Learning in music stimulates students’ curiosity and creativity, and enables personal expression through sound. Performing, listening and composing music contributes to cognitive development, memory and wellbeing.

Developing aural awareness is foundational to music education, and listening is integral to all musical experiences. Listening skills include the ability to focus on, hear, understand and respond to musical stimuli and discriminate between sounds. For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, listening may include the use of assistive technology, or accessing music through touch or sight.

In Stage 2, as students engage in performing music, they develop posture, position, technique and auditory processing. It is important for students to develop vocalisation, intonation, vocabulary, connectedness and musical competence through singing. By engaging with music repertoire from a wide selection of cultural contexts and historical periods, students develop understandings of ways to use the elements of music in their own compositions.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Students build on the language and vocabulary of the elements of music to form connections about how sounds are organised, how musical ideas are created and how to respond to different genres of music across cultures.  

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers focus on the following aspects of the elements of music in Stage 2.

Element of musicKey questionsExample
Duration

The lengths of sounds and silences in music.		How can you use body percussion in different ways to show the beat or rhythm patterns?Beat, groupings, metre or time signature, rhythm patterns, ostinato, tempo, note values, rests, presto (very fast), moderato (moderately), largo (very slow).
Pitch

The relative highness or lowness of sounds.		What can you add to the melody to make it different?Melody, melodic contour, harmony.
Texture

The way layers of sound are combined in a piece of music.		Can you describe the layers of sounds in this section?Layers of sounds, unison, solo, accompaniment.
Performing media

The instruments/voices/sound sources used in a piece of music.		What is the role of each sound source in this music?Brass, keyboard, acoustic, electronic, digital sounds, world instruments.
Timbre

The distinctive quality of a sound.		How would you describe the differences in sound quality between wind and brass instruments?​

Majestic, bold, vocal quality,  sound quality, instrumental groups, world instruments.


Dynamics

The volume of sound.		What techniques can you use to control the volume of the sound when you’re singing or playing?Piano (soft), forte (loud), crescendo (getting louder), decrescendo/diminuendo (getting softer).
Expression

The musical detail that articulates a style or the interpretation of a style.		How can you adjust your singing or playing to change the mood?Playful, serious, relaxing.
Structure

The design or form in music. It refers to how a composition is constructed in sections or parts.		How are the sections in this music related to one another?

Phrases (musical sentences), introduction, sections, patterns, repetition, rounds, coda, AB and ABA forms.


The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

In Stage 2, students consider the compositions and Practices of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander musicians and observe protocols. Students deepen their understanding of how Cultural Knowledges are communicated through music and sound.

Performing: Music is performed to communicate musical ideas in various ways

It is important to select singing and playing repertoire from a wide variety of musical styles. Students experience and learn vocal repertoire through echo singing, partner songs, 2-part and 3-part rounds or songs with verses and a chorus. Body percussion and clapping games can add layers and develop confidence in part singing, rounds and songs in unison. Adding percussion reinforces students’ listening skills as they engage with multiple musical ideas.

Encourage students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing to feel their throat or diaphragm when they sing so they can feel the vibrations. Use instruments that produce clean sounds when accompanying a singer, and explore digital colour coding to highlight lyrics when singing.

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs for peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups for the wider school community.

Listening: Musical ideas are conveyed in various ways using the elements of music

Students continue to develop aural awareness and auditory memory through listening. Body percussion and movement support students to listen actively and develop musical understanding.

Use simple graphic or staff notation as a system to visually represent musical ideas and map sounds to symbols. This supports students to communicate musical ideas.

Image long description: A diagram demonstrating the relationship of types of notes. A whole note (semibreve) sits at the top and splits into 2 half notes (minims) sitting beneath it. The half notes split into 4 quarter notes (crotchets) sitting beneath them, and these split into 8 eighth notes (quavers). The eighth notes split into 16 sixteenth notes (semiquavers) at the bottom.

Image long description: A pair of musical staves. The top one uses a treble clef and records each note from the top line (F) down to an additional line below the stave (middle C). The bottom stave starts with a note on the last line of the stave (G), continuing up to the additional line above the stave and meeting the same middle C as the treble clef stave.

Some students may need to use multisensory tools or props (for example, cups and sticks) to learn about notation.

When experiencing music from historical periods or cultures around the world, students may access events, maps or images to support their understanding of contexts. Students draw on personal experiences as they describe and explain music. When comparing musical works teachers may ask:

  • What is similar about this music compared to the other piece that was played?
  • What is different about this music compared to the other piece?
  • What does each piece of music help us to understand about the context of when and where it was created or performed?

Composing: Music is composed to communicate musical ideas in various ways

Students explore ways to communicate musical ideas when composing by:

  • experimenting and selecting different combinations of sound sources to explore timbres and moods
  • varying melody or rhythm patterns, using repetition or contrast
  • exploring different sound sources, singing or playing techniques and varying volume (dynamic levels)
  • creating new lyrics to a song or verse to reinforce structure
  • creating music to represent a storyline.

Students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing can be supported through:

  • using a communication board of symbols to share their intentions for creating their own music
  • working in a quieter location or in a one-on-one setting, if required
  • using headphones to ensure the quality of sounds.

Vocabulary: composition, coda, improvise, metre, rehearse, repertoire, staff notation, syncopation, technique.

  • Partitioned fractions A: Model and represent unit fractions, and their multiples, to a complete whole on a number line

Why is it important? 

Visual arts have provided a means of communication, creative expression and representation in cultures around the world and throughout history. Learning in Visual Arts develops students’ understanding of the relationships between artists, artworks, the world and audiences. In Visual Arts students explore the ways materials, techniques and processes are used to represent subject matter and ideas in artworks.  

In Stage 2, it is important for students to choose ways to use materials, techniques and the elements of art and design to represent ideas about their world in their artworks. Students develop understandings of the practices of artists as they explore artworks from various cultural contexts and historical periods. By exhibiting their own artworks, students gain a deeper understanding of how artworks are experienced and interpreted by audiences. 

Supporting language and vocabulary development 

Vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language of visual arts, including the vocabulary of the elements of art and design, provides the foundations for learning. Students develop the vocabulary necessary to reflect on their own artmaking experiences and to describe artworks from a range of contexts.  

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions related to artworks they are making or appreciating. See the table below for examples. 

Concepts Key questions Vocabulary examples 
Artist 

How will you plan and document your art making? 

What do you notice about the artist’s style and how do you think they created those effects? 

Annotate, blend, convey, digital tools, document, effects, film, plan, printmaking, process, represent, rubbing, style, tools. 
Artwork 

How did you use the drawing materials to create texture and tone in your artwork? 

What do you notice about the scale and proportions in this artwork? 

Analogous colours, balance, complementary colours, composition, images, properties, proportion, scale, textiles, texture, tone.  
World 

What subject matter or ideas about the world do you want to represent in your artwork? 

How has the artist been influenced by their own personal, social or cultural context? 

Context, cultural, ideas, subject matter. 
Audience 

How will you communicate ideas about your artwork in a display or exhibit? 

What do the signs and symbols in this artwork communicate to the audience? 

Audience, communicate, display, interpretation, meaning, physical, protocols, virtual display. 

The following English content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes: 

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding 
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication forms.  

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities   

In Stage 2, students explore artmaking processes and deepen their understanding of the significance of visual arts to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. They develop knowledge and understanding of the importance of protocols in expressing Cultural information. 

Making: Artists represent their world through subject matter and ideas in artworks 

Students engage in making artworks to represent their own interpretations of the world through art forms. They choose ways to develop ideas using materials, techniques and the elements of art and design. As part of the artmaking process, students sketch ideas and annotate samples of work, or document their art making in an art journal, recording their ideas and plans for ways to refine their artworks. 

Students represent subject matter and ideas through drawing by exploring techniques such as observational, contour or gestural drawing. For example, students may use observational drawing techniques to draw animals, plants, objects or sites to connect to learning in other areas of the curriculum. They might make botanical drawings to connect to learning in Science and Technology or illustrations of historical sources in HSIE. Teachers can support students to use their observational skills by reminding them to closely observe the subject matter they are drawing – to draw what they notice. Keep in mind that observations can involve a range of senses. Students can experiment with various drawing materials on a selection of surfaces to create textural and tonal effect. For example, they can use a range of HB–8B pencils, pens or charcoal on plain, patterned, smooth or textured papers. Drawing may include the use of digital software or assistive technologies, including eye gaze technology. 

Students may engage in art making using art forms inspired by artists or artworks they have explored in art appreciation. For example, students may make weavings inspired by Latin American textiles. Weavings may be made using a variety of materials such as string, wool, rope, strips of fabric or upcycled materials.  

Some students, including those with low vision or who are blind, may require adjustments to make artworks. This could include using materials with different tactile qualities and media to allow for deeper exploration and creation. Students should be allowed to interact with artistic materials through different senses; for example, touching the different textures, smelling the materials or listening to the sounds materials make when manipulated. 

Appreciating: Artists convey meaning about their world in artworks which can be experienced and interpreted by audiences 

As students explore artworks from cultural contexts and historical periods around the world, they begin to understand how artists are influenced by people, time and place, and how artworks convey ideas about an artist’s world. Students build an understanding of how artworks are experienced and interpreted in different ways by audiences. 

For example, students can compare artworks from historical periods to describe: 

  • subject matter or ideas (for example, human figures or animal forms) 
  • art form, materials, techniques, processes (for example, porcelain sculpture or engraved print) 
  • elements of art and design (for example, tone, shape, composition) 
  • signs and symbols (for example, spiritual or religious motifs).

Students make associations between artworks and their own contexts by considering ways that artworks connect to: 

  • Personal contexts: What experiences, emotions or perspectives of the artist’s world are represented in the artwork? How does the artwork connect to your world? 
  • Social contexts: What social experiences or historical events of triumph or struggle are represented in the artwork?  
  • Cultural contexts: How does the artwork reflect the cultural traditions of a place? In what ways does your context influence your art making? 

Exhibiting: Displays and exhibitions of artworks communicate ideas about artists’ practices to audiences 

Students begin to make more intentional choices about ways to display and exhibit their own artworks. They may take photographs during the artmaking process to demonstrate their thinking and ways of working or they may choose to exhibit a completed artwork. They can begin to consider alternatives that will enhance the way their work is understood, such as by elevating a sculptural form on a box or stand, hanging a textile work so it can be viewed from multiple angles, or creating an installation outdoors. 

Students can investigate physical exhibitions and virtual displays to explore ways artworks are displayed according to the environment. They may observe the way artworks are displayed in a gallery, museum, public space, sculpture garden or cafe. They may observe the ways placement, lighting, artist statements or background information about the artist and the artwork contribute to understanding for an audience. 

Teachers may prompt students to reflect on their journey through the artmaking process by supporting them to recognise their successes and challenges. They may ask questions such as: 

  • What part of your artwork do you think is the most successful? 
  • What creative risks did you take in your art making? 
  • What challenges did you encounter as you were making your artwork? 

Some students may require adjustments to view and exhibit artworks. Some adjustments could include experiencing artworks that are accompanied by sounds or auditory support; for example, music or auditory descriptions. 

Vocabulary: 2D art form, 3D art form, art form, asymmetry, background, colour wheel, complementary colour, contour, contrast, cross hatching, digital, emphasis, exhibition, foreground, gestural, hatching, landscape, middle ground, monoprint, observational, perspective, printmaking, real or implied texture, relief print, sculptor, shading, stippling, symmetry, technologies, textiles, virtual, weaving. 

Making connections through related content  

Mathematics:  

  • Two-dimensional spatial structure A: 2D shapes: Transform shapes by reflecting, translating and rotating 

Human Society and its Environment:  

  • History uses sources to construct narratives of the past: Sources provide evidence of how people lived in the past: Mesoamerica and the Andes; Sources provide evidence of how people lived in the first penal settlement at Sydney Cove 

Science and Technology:  

  • Physical and living systems depend on energy: Living things depend on energy and materials to survive

Why is it important?

Drama is a practice of embodied storytelling and a form of communication in cultures around the world. Humans have an innate desire to explore the way people interact with one another and the world. Drama experiences widen students’ understandings of people and relationships as they explore situations from different perspectives. Students develop empathy as they experience what it feels like to ‘walk in someone else’s shoes’.

In Stage 3, students use their imagination to generate original ideas for characters and dramatic action in response to the world around them. They begin to use dramatic symbols in performances to shape shared meaning for an audience. Students’ understanding of the world is enriched as they experience drama from cultural and historical contexts around the world and make associations with their own contexts.

Some students with disability may need adjustments to access and participate in dramatic experiences. This could include adjustments to support movement, communication, access to the drama space, sensory experiences and collaboration with others.

The Creative Arts K–6 Drama focus area builds foundational understandings that are further developed in the Drama 7–10 Syllabus (2023).

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching language and vocabulary of the dramatic elements provides the foundations for learning in the context of drama.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following dramatic elements in Stage 3.

Dramatic elementFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Role

Points of view, objects or personas presented through embodiment.		Why did you choose to enact this role?

In what ways do relationships between roles influence the ways the characters developed and changed?		Archetype, stereotype.
Character

A dramatic role built with complexity, personality and/or background. 		How would you describe the attitude of your character?

How did the performers communicate ideas about status and power in the drama?		Status, authority, personality, intention, attitude, protagonist.
Tension

The energy that drives drama. Tension can be developed through embodiment, structure, problems, tasks, conflict and manipulation of audience expectations.		How can you build and resolve tension between the characters?

How did the performers manipulate dramatic tension?		Energy, mystery, problem, dilemma, resolution.
Situation

The circumstances characters experience and that shape their actions and intentions.		How can you devise a dramatic situation by adapting the circumstances of a known story?

How did the characters resolve the tension in the situation?		Circumstances, context, social event, environmental event.
Space

The shape and spatial design of the performance area, and the spatial dynamics and relationships between performers, performance area and audience.		How will the characters move and interact with one another within the performance space?

How did the characters create a sense of belief in the way they used the space?		Performance space, imagined space, distance, stage geography.
Time

The transformation of the real time of the audience to the imagined time of the performance.		How can you create a still image to capture a moment in time?

How did the performers demonstrate they were moving backwards and forwards in time?		Moment in time, transition, historical time.
Structure

The way a dramatic work is shaped, which can include cause and effect, narrative, plot, and sequencing of images, motifs or ideas.		How can you re-sequence the narrative to go back in time?

What clues did you observe during the performance that prepared you for the end result?		Cause and effect, sequencing of ideas.
Language

Ways of expressing and receiving images, ideas, feelings and stories, using spoken, visual, written and/or gestural communication strategies.		How will you use voice or language to reflect the individual qualities of your character?

How did the actors use gesture and silence to communicate ideas?		Expression, intonation, gesture, silence, cultural language.
Atmosphere

The feeling or mood created through dramatic action.		How could you use colour in the costumes to represent mood?

How were lighting and sound manipulated to change the atmosphere during the performance?		Atmosphere, mood, lighting, tense, ominous.
Symbol

An object, action, character, image or sound that can represent an idea, action or feeling on a conscious or subconscious level.		How could you use an everyday object to communicate a symbolic idea?

What recurring symbols did you observe in the performance?		Symbol, metaphor, literal, object, image, icon.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words
  • Understanding and responding to literature: Characterisation

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in this focus area supports students to appreciate the intent of dramatic works as performed by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. Students continue to learn why protocols are required when engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dramatic works.

Making: Drama is made using the dramatic elements to shape meaning

Students investigate more complex ways to combine the dramatic elements to shape meaning for an audience. They explore ways to indicate the time of day, a historical period or transitions in time using:

  • movements or actions (for example, waking up, yawning or looking at a watch)
  • language (for example, ‘It’s almost midnight’, ‘It’s time to go to school’ or ‘I’ll meet you for dinner’)
  • costumes (for example, pyjamas at bedtime, a uniform at school, or a work outfit or uniform at work)
  • objects (for example, a lunchbox for lunchtime, a briefcase for work or a parasol for a historical period)
  • sounds (for example, an alarm clock or school bell, or birds chirping).

Dramatic tension and atmosphere can be established through dramatic elements such as character, space and time. Teachers may prompt students by asking:

  • How can you use silence, stillness or movement instead of language to communicate tension to the audience?
  • How can you use elements of production, such as lighting, sound or digital technologies to manipulate tension or atmosphere?

Metaphor and symbol are used to enrich and extend dramatic meaning. Dramatic symbols may include:

  • Objects (for example, a treasure box to represent something precious, or a book to represent knowledge)
  • Sounds (for example, a siren to represent an emergency or a chime to represent a magic spell)
  • Characters (for example, a map to represent an explorer, or a handshake between 2 characters to represent an agreement).

Symbols require background knowledge. Some EAL/D learners may need explicit teaching to connect symbols to their representations. Students should be encouraged to share familiar symbols that represent people, places and ideas.

Performing: Drama is performed using the dramatic elements to shape meaning for audiences  

As students become more experienced with performing they make more deliberate choices about ways to enact characters, situations and stories. They rehearse and refine performances to prepare for an audience. Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs to peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups to the wider school community.

To convey ideas and engage audiences students can use simple elements of production such as:

  • set design (for example, a picnic chair or tableware)
  • costumes (for example, a crown or jacket)
  • props (for example, a magnifying glass or an umbrella)
  • lighting (for example, a lamp or torch)
  • sound (for example, music or a phone ringing)
  • technologies (for example, recorded sounds such as animals or traffic).

Teachers can assist students to reflect on their experiences and contributions as drama makers and performers by asking:

  • How did your character change and evolve over the rehearsal and performance periods?
  • How did you use voice, language and movement to reflect the personality and attitudes of your character and to create atmosphere?
  • What symbols did you incorporate to shape meaning for the audience?

Appreciating: Drama is influenced by the context it is made and performed in and is understood by audiences in various ways

As students explore drama from around the world they recognise that drama conveys meaning about historical, cultural, social and personal contexts. Students build understandings about the relationships between drama makers, contexts and audiences. They investigate the intentions of dramatic practitioners and how the dramatic elements are used to shape meaning.

Students extend their understanding of drama by comparing historical and contemporary drama forms and styles. Teachers may provide background information about key features of drama practices.

Teachers may prompt students as they investigate drama by asking:

  • How did the performers use the dramatic elements to convey ideas?
  • How were the elements of production used to shape meaning for the audience?
  • What type of tension did you feel in this drama? What aspects of the story or characters made you feel this tension?
  • How does the form or style of drama in this context vary from other drama traditions around the world?

Vocabulary: archetype, atmosphere, attitude, authority, circumstances, context, dilemma, dramatic elements, elements of performance, intention, lighting, metaphor, moment, mood, mystery, personality, protagonist, resolution, stage geography, status, stereotype, symbol, transition.

Making connections through related content

English K–10:

  • Understanding and responding to literature: Narrative; Characterisation; Imagery, symbol and connotation; Perspective and context

content.value:
Why is it important?

Music is a form of personal and cultural expression and a way of connecting through sound and silence. Music has occupied a significant place in cultures around the world throughout time. Learning in music stimulates students’ curiosity, creativity and enables personal expression through sound. Performing, listening and composing music contributes to cognitive development, memory and wellbeing.

Developing aural awareness is foundational to music education, and listening is integral to all musical experiences. Listening skills include the ability to focus on, hear, understand and respond to musical stimuli and discriminate between sounds. For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, listening may include the use of assistive technology, or accessing music through touch or sight.

In Stage 3, students collaboratively perform and compose music to communicate musical ideas. Students’ understandings are enriched as they investigate repertoires from cultural traditions around the world and develop understandings about the ways music connects people across time and place.

Stage 3 includes a Creating written texts outcome and focus area that applies to learning across the Creative Arts syllabus. Specific content in the Creating written texts focus area supports students to create written texts to develop understandings in the Creative Arts K–6 syllabus.

The Creative Arts K–6 Music focus area builds foundational understandings that are further developed in the Music 7–10 Syllabus (2024).

Supporting vocabulary development

Students build on vocabulary of the elements of music to form connections about how sounds are created, organised or performed and how to respond to different genres of music across time and cultures.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers focus on the following aspects of the elements of music in Stage 3.

Elements of musicKey questionsVocabulary examples
Duration

The lengths of sounds and silences in music.		Is this rhythm or tempo representative of music from a particular style, culture, time or place?Presto (very fast), moderato (moderate), largo (very slow), accelerando (getting faster), ritardando (getting slower), syncopation.
Pitch

The relative highness or lowness of sounds.		How can you represent the shape or contour of the melody?High/low and repeated sounds, melody patterns, melodic phrase, steps and leaps, major/minor chords, drone, harmony, riff.
Texture

The way layers of sound are combined in a piece of music.		How could you manipulate the texture to add layers to your composition?Thin or thick, melodic/rhythmic/harmonic layers, solo, accompaniment.
Performing media

The instruments/voices/sound sources used in a piece of music.		What is the role of each of the sound sources in the music?Vocal music, orchestral instruments, world instruments, acoustic, electronic, digitally edited.
Timbre

The distinctive quality of a sound.		How many different timbres can you produce using your voice/ instrument?Nasal, metallic, rich, smooth, harsh.

Dynamics

The volume of sound.

 

How do the volume changes impact the mood of the music?Crescendo/decrescendo/diminuendo (gradations/changes in volume), fortissimo (very loud), pianissimo (very quiet), mezzo forte (moderately loud) and mezzo piano (moderately quiet).
Expression

The musical detail that articulates a style or the interpretation of a style.		How can sound sources influence expression?Mysterious, dark, bright or light mood.

Pizzicato (plucked), staccato (short and sharp), legato (smooth).
Structure

The design or form in music. It refers to how a composition is constructed in sections or parts.		How do the sections of the music compare or contrast with each other?AB (binary), ABA (ternary), ABACA (rondo), 12-bar blues, bridge, improvised.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in this focus area provides students with opportunities to investigate the contemporary ways Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People share music to strengthen and maintain their Cultures. Students continue to learn why protocols are required when engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander music.

Performing: Music is performed using the elements of music to communicate musical ideas

Music is performed and made by organising sound through singing, moving and playing. Engaging in collaborative performance activities – singing or playing – builds an understanding of the elements of music to communicate musical ideas. Performing chants, 2-part or 3-part rounds, songs with harmonies or in unison with or without accompaniment supports students to understand musical structure and texture.

Improvising and innovating on known pieces through melody and rhythm, or dynamics and expression, encourages students to shape their performance in expressive ways. Explore different ways of sharing original ideas within a performance via a short vocal or instrumental solo, improvisation, body percussion or through call and response techniques as a class or in pairs.

Performing for an audience develops rehearsal skills, accuracy, expression, performance skills and collaboration. Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs for peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups for the wider school community. Performers can appear before live audiences or in digital recordings shared with the school community.

Constructive feedback using musical vocabulary is important for students to understand ways to further develop their musical understanding and performance skills and to celebrate successes and achievements.

Listening: Music is influenced by the context in which it is performed and composed

Students use listening skills to investigate repertoire in a range of cultural and historical styles to develop their own aural awareness. They identify how musical ideas are created and performed in various ways, according to context, and begin to understand the importance and value of music for all cultures throughout history. Listening is integrated with all aspects of learning in music and is fundamental to all performing and composing activities. Students interpret and create their own graphic notation to represent musical ideas they listen to.

Image long description: An example of graphic notation with a line that gradually rises and falls. The line dips slightly before rising to a peak, followed by a slight trough, then a higher peak that falls away slightly.

Some students may need to be supported to learn about notation through the use of multisensory tools or props, for example cups and sticks.

Using listening skills to compare and contrast music in various genres and styles provides students with opportunities to reason and think critically about how musical ideas are expressed using the elements of music. Students also develop listening skills through collaborating when performing various forms and styles of music, or when composing for different purposes.

By investigating the context of when and where a piece of music was performed or composed, students develop an understanding that music is impacted by time and place. Support students to think about context by experiencing, performing or asking:

  • Where could the music come from?
  • When was it first composed or performed?
  • Was the music written for a particular reason?
  • What else was going on in the world at the time, and did this influence the music?
  • How does the composer use the elements of music, such as pitch and dynamics, to convey a theme or message?

Composing: Music is composed using the elements of music to communicate musical ideas

Composing focuses on organising sounds to sing or play music and may include innovating on standard repertoire or creating original musical compositions. Students may use voice, body percussion, a variety of sound sources, instruments or digital technologies to improvise, organise, manipulate and record sounds.

Modelling and providing opportunities for students to experiment with rearranging and improvising through singing and playing will develop their skills in composing. Working with partners or small groups to generate and document ideas and layer sounds provides scaffolds to support students’ confidence and expression.

Students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing can be supported through:

  • using a communication board of symbols to share their intentions for creating their own music
  • working in a quieter location or in a one-on-one setting, if required
  • using headphones to ensure the quality of sounds.

Vocabulary: accelerando, acoustic, Baroque, bridge, call and response, chord, Classical, composer, contemporary, digital, drone, electronic, groove, hook, jazz, Medieval, orchestra, performer, phrases, rap, recording, riff, ritardando, rock, Romantic.

Making connections through related content

English K–10:

  • Creating written texts: Informative purposes; Text features for multiple purposes; Sentence-level grammar; Word-level language

content.value:
Why is it important?

Visual arts have provided a means of communication, creative expression and representation around the world and throughout history. Learning in Visual Arts enables students to engage with materials, techniques and processes to represent subject matter and ideas in artworks. Students develop a complex understanding of artworld concepts and the relationships between artists, artworks, the world and audiences.

Image long description: The terms 'Artist', 'World' and 'Audience', connected by a circle, are each positioned on a vertex of a triangle which is sits within the circle. The term 'Artwork' sits in the centre of the triangle and is connected by 3 lines to each vertex demonstrating a connection to the other terms.

In Stage 3, students develop intentionality in their artmaking practice. They explore how artists are influenced by contexts and how they make artworks to communicate intentional ideas to audiences. Students explore the ways in which artworks are curated and exhibited to construct meaning for audiences, enabling audiences to interpret and critique artworks in various ways. Learning experiences in Making, Appreciating and Exhibiting are interrelated in Visual Arts, and work together to develop students’ knowledge, skills and understanding.

The Creative Arts K–6 focus area Visual Arts builds foundational understandings that are further developed in the Visual Arts 7–10 Syllabus (2024).

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language of visual arts, including the vocabulary of the elements of art and design, provides the foundations for learning. Students develop the vocabulary necessary to reflect on their own artmaking experiences and to describe artworks from a range of contexts.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions related to artworks they are making or appreciating see the table below for examples.

Artworld conceptsKey questionsVocabulary examples
ArtistWhat materials, techniques and processes will you use to make your artwork?

How has the artist used digital technologies to complement their traditional art practices?		4D art form, animation, artist’s intention, artmaking practice, choice, engraving, multimodal artwork, performance work, photography, process.
ArtworkHow do you intend to represent your ideas in your artwork?

How has the composition of this artwork been arranged?		Composition, conventions, emphasis, hollow, horizon line, one-point perspective, opaque/transparent/translucent colours, repetition, representation, rhythm, solid, structural, surface.
WorldHow can you represent your own ideas or perspectives of the world in your artwork?

How did the cultural context or historical period influence the way the artist made this artwork?		Art historical period, artist’s viewpoint, belief, contemporary, cultural, imaginative, realistic, subjective, symbolic, value, viewpoint.
AudienceHow will you use the elements of art and design, including signs or symbols, in your artwork to convey ideas to an audience?

What ideas do you think the artist was intending to convey to an audience through their artwork?		Art historian, curator, documentation, elements of art and design, installation, interpret, mood, site-specific work.

The following English content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes:

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

In Stage 3, students investigate the contemporary ways in which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples maintain Cultural Connection through art making. Students gain further insight into the importance of protocols when engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art.

Making: Artists represent their world in intentional ways through their artmaking practice

Through the practice of making artworks, students explore the relationships between artist, artwork, world and audience. When students engage as artists to make artworks, they explore materials, techniques, processes, art forms, and the elements of art and design. They learn about ways to represent subject matter and ideas about their world in intentional ways through their artmaking practice. They learn to demonstrate how artists, artworks, the world and audiences have influenced their own artmaking practice.

Students may draw inspiration for their art making from artists or artworks they have explored in art appreciation, or connect their art making to topics or themes being explored in other learning areas. For example, students may make artworks of realistic, imaginative or symbolic birds inspired by their learning about animals and their habitats in Science and Technology.
