Teachers play an important role in supporting students to develop their intentions for an artwork. It is important for students to explore their own ideas, considering factors such as identity, points of view, beliefs or perspectives.

Before making artworks, students can plan, sketch ideas or create annotated illustrations to support art making. It is important for teachers to give students choice in their art making, allowing them to select their own materials, techniques, processes and art forms to represent their ideas in particular ways. Students may consider alternative ways to represent their ideas using the available resources.

Some students, including those with low vision or who are blind, may require adjustments to make artworks. This could include allowing them to use materials with different tactile qualities and media to enable deeper exploration and creation. Students should be allowed to interact with artistic materials through different senses; for example, touching the different textures, smelling the materials or listening to the sounds materials make when manipulated.

Appreciating: Artists are influenced by contexts and make artworks that audiences can critique and interpret in various ways

Students observe artworks from around the world and investigate artists’ practices from a wide selection of cultural contexts and historical periods. Exploring historical artworks provides a window to other times and places, and supports students to develop understanding and perspectives of contemporary experiences. Students compare artworks from historical and contemporary contexts to understand significant influences on artists and artmaking practices over time. They may draw from their own experiences to connect with different artworks.

Students engage as an audience by experiencing and connecting with artworks, artists, galleries and museums through incursions, excursions or virtual experiences. They may observe reproductions of artworks through postcards, books, posters or online exhibitions. Students learn to critique and interpret artworks by accessing, investigating and researching artists and artworks.

Teachers may provide students with some background information about an artist or artwork, including details about the cultural context or historical time frame. Information may include:

  • the title of the artwork and name of the artist(s)
  • materials, techniques and processes used in the artwork
  • the location of the artwork
  • cultural context (for example, the cultural origins of the artist)
  • historical timeframe (for example, the year the artwork was made and what was happening in the world at that time).

Developing the ability to closely observe artworks supports students’ own artmaking practice. They develop agency as they apply their observational skills to represent intention in their art making. When planning appreciating experiences, it is important to select types of artworks that make connections with students’ own art making.

Exhibiting: Artworks are displayed and curated in various ways to communicate intentional ideas to audiences

A student’s practice in exhibiting reinforces their art making and appreciating experiences. It is important that students learn how to curate images and convey messages for a particular audience, and how to critique and interpret artworks within their context.

Students can explore the ways in which artists and curators construct meaning through displays and exhibitions. They may explore exhibition spaces in their local community and discuss the curator’s role in assembling a narrative for audiences to engage with as they construct personal and cultural interpretations.

Teachers may model ways to display or curate artworks to communicate intentional ideas to an audience. Students can curate their own and other students’ works, displaying them in ways that allow for various interpretations. Exhibiting provides students with an opportunity to follow the artmaking practice from conception to realisation.

It is important that students learn how to responsibly and ethically acknowledge the work of an artist when accessing and referring to an artwork.

Some students may require adjustments to view and exhibit artworks. This could include experiencing artworks that are accompanied by sounds or auditory support; for example, music or auditory descriptions.

Vocabulary: 4D art form, art movement, audience, balance, charcoal, composition, contemporary, curator, document, emphasis, engraving, harmony, hollow, horizon line, installation, intention, mixed media, mood, movement, multimodal, opaque, perspective, photography, proportion, repetition, representation, rhythm, scale, solid, surface, translucent, transparent, upcycled materials.

  • Historical sources present perspectives on the past: People have developed Australia as a nation

  • Knowledge of our world and beyond inspires sustainable solutions: Living things may change over millions of years, in response to their environments

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Dance is a distinct form of movement that is universal to the human experience. Throughout time, dance has brought people together to share knowledge, culture and ideas. In dance, students use the body as an instrument to express and communicate ideas.

In Stage 3, students extend and connect their understanding of the elements of dance to compose and perform a group-devised dance for an audience. They investigate dance from a wide selection of cultural, historical and contemporary contexts that influence their artistic choices in their own dance practice.

As a movement-based artform, dance is beneficial to motor development, strength, and physical and emotional wellbeing. All bodies are diverse and move in different ways. Some students with physical disability may require adjustments, including assistive devices such as walkers or wheelchairs. Adjustments can be made to the environment, equipment and instructions to create an inclusive learning environment.

The Creative Arts K–6 Dance focus area builds foundational understandings that are further developed in the Dance 7–10 Syllabus (2023).

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language and vocabulary of the elements of dance – space, time and dynamics – helps students understand and describe dance as they learn to compose, perform and appreciate it.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following elements of dance in Stage 3.

Element of danceFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Space

The components of space, including shape, level, direction, dimension, pathways, floor patterns and stage space.		How can you create a pathway of movement to communicate your ideas and intent?

How did the performers adapt the shapes and movements in the dance to convey intent?		Low, moderate or high levels; direction; pathway.
Time

The components of time, including metre, rhythm, accent, tempo, duration and stillness.		How will you convey your ideas through the rhythm of your movements?

How did the performers use steady or irregular movements to convey ideas?		Slower, faster, increasing, decreasing tempo; longer or shorter duration; steady or irregular rhythm.
Dynamics

The release of energy, weight and/or force over a period of time to create movement qualities.		How will you transfer your weight to adjust the force of your movements in the dance?

How did the dancers use dynamics to convey ideas and intent?		Soft, heavy, sharp, sudden, staccato, soft, delicate, free-flowing movements.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Interacting; Listening for understanding
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

The content in Stage 3 provides opportunities for students to explore how Cultural identity is strengthened through dance practices. Students further develop their understanding of protocols and the requirements surrounding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dance.

Composing: Dance is composed using the elements of dance to generate movements that communicate ideas and intent

Teachers can support students in developing ideas for a dance composition by providing a stimulus that might interest the group. Teachers may also suggest themes or topics connected to learning in other subject areas, such as stories from poetry, literature, events or situations.

Students can brainstorm and discuss ideas using mind maps or storyboards. They develop dance sequences using the elements of dance to express ideas connected to their chosen aspect of the topic, such as:

  • Space (for example, changing level, direction or pathway of movement to reflect interactions between characters in a story)
  • Time (for example, responding to the rhythms in music to express the changing movement of water)
  • Dynamics (for example, making sharp, hurried or exaggerated movements to represent environmental events).

As students develop confidence in conveying their ideas through dance, they begin drawing on dances from different times and places and their own personal and cultural contexts to compose their own dance. This could include sharing personal cultural experiences of dance.

Teachers play an important role in ensuring students develop safe dance practices by engaging in warm-up and cool-down exercises, and following procedures and protocols.

Performing: Dance is performed using the elements of dance to communicate ideas and intent to audiences

Rehearsing dance sequences provides students with opportunities to reflect on their own performance and receive feedback from one another or the teacher. As students rehearse dance they are able to consider ways to refine and strengthen their composition using the elements of dance to communicate their intent. Teachers may prompt students with questions such as:

  • How are you able to improve your dance technique through control and balance?
  • How can you use costumes or props to enhance meaning in your dance? (For example, using scarves or ribbons to create larger shapes.)
  • Is the dance communicating your intended message, story or idea?
  • What decisions did you make as a choreographer or dancer?

Performing dance for a small or large live audience, or digitally recording performances, provides students with rich opportunities to apply their growing understanding of ways to communicate ideas and intent using the elements of dance.

Appreciating: Dance is influenced by the context it is composed and performed in and is understood by audiences in various ways

As students explore dance from around the world, they recognise that dance conveys meaning in historical, cultural, social and personal contexts. Students may draw from their own experiences to connect with different dance works. They build an understanding of the relationships between dancers, choreographers, contexts and audiences. Students investigate the intentions of the choreographer and how the elements of dance are used to enhance an audience’s understanding.

Ask students to consider:

  • Who are the choreographers and dancers?
  • When and where was this dance performed?
  • What was the purpose of the dance?
  • How does this dance contribute to maintaining a sense of cultural identity and belonging for the dancers and audience?

Vocabulary: alignment, artistic, audience, balance, control stage, duration, element theatre, intent, pathway, performance, quality, rehearse, spin, staccato, unfold, theatrical, weight.

Making connections through related content

PDHPE:

  • Movement skill and physical activity: Create, communicate and collaborate in physical activities; Refining fundamental movement skills enhances health and wellbeing

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Dance is a distinct form of movement that is universal to the human experience. Throughout time, dance has brought people together to share knowledge, culture and ideas. In dance, students use their bodies as instruments to express and communicate ideas.

In Early Stage 1, it is important for students to develop an awareness of personal space and explore ways to make body shapes and movements, linking them into simple sequences. They recognise that dance is performed in a range of contexts by observing dance from cultural contexts around the world.

As a movement-based artform, dance is beneficial to motor development, strength, and physical and emotional wellbeing. All bodies are diverse and move in different ways. Some students with a physical disability may require adjustments, including assistive devices such as walkers or wheelchairs. Adjustments can be made to the environment, equipment and instructions to create an inclusive learning environment.

There are opportunities for connection with PDHPE Movement skill and physical activity content, particularly regarding spatial awareness, balance, and participating in physical activities that provide enjoyment and motivation to be physically active.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the vocabulary of shapes, movements and the elements of dance provides the foundations for learning. Students develop the vocabulary necessary to reflect on their own dance experiences and to describe dance in a range of contexts.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following elements of dance in Early Stage 1.

Element of danceFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Space
The components of space, including shape, level, direction, dimension, pathways, floor patterns and stage space.		What kinds of shapes can you make with your body?

How can you make movements at a low level?

How did the dancers change the level or direction of movements?		Shape: pointed, curved, angular.

Level: high, low.



Direction: up, down, forwards, backwards.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

English K–10:

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions; Understanding and using grammar when interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Early Stage 1 content provides students with opportunities to develop curiosity, creativity and imagination by appreciating Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends represented in dance.

Composing and performing: Dance is made and performed using shapes and movements

In Early Stage 1, students explore ways to make body shapes and movements at different levels and in different directions within a designated space. They begin to experiment with ways to link shapes and movements into a sequence.

It is important for students to develop safe dance practices by performing warming up and cooling down exercises. Establishing routines and signals (e.g. a sound or gesture) helps prepare students to engage in dance experiences including start, stop, stand still and sit down.

Dance games, such as musical statues, support students to explore making shapes and movements. For example, students may create shapes and movements while the music is playing and freeze in a shape when the music stops.

Students explore ways to move their body by responding to teacher prompts, such as:

  • How can you move different body parts at the same time or in isolation? (For example, arms and legs, shoulders or fingers.)
  • How can you move your body in different ways? (For example, fast and slow, high and low, forwards and backwards.)
  • What kinds of locomotor/non-locomotor movements can you make? (For example, jump, side gallop, roll, bend, stretch, twist.)

Teachers may use prompts, such as flashcards, to indicate types of shapes and movements. These may include arrows, symbols, images or objects to indicate direction or level of movement, or types of body shapes.

Image long description: 2 arrows indicating direction or level of movement. The first points to the right and the second points up.

Image long description: Symbols of stars and moons to indicate types of body shapes that can be created and connected into a simple sequence.

Students connect individual dance shapes and movements into a simple sequence and perform a dance with other students by:

  • linking shapes and movements developed during composing experiences (for example, demonstrating the ways living things move by crawling, flying or swimming, to connect to learning in Science and Technology)
  • creating patterns by linking shapes (for example, repeating a pattern of high and low movements).

Appreciating: Dance can be experienced and described

Students make connections to the contexts in which they have seen or experienced dance in their lives. By engaging with dance from cultures and contexts around the world, students are provided with a window to observe dance in a range of places over time. Students may experience dance through live or recorded performances and school performances by peers. Students begin to recognise they can express their own ideas and feelings in response to dance.

Students may respond to questions such as:

  • Where was the dance performed?
  • How would you describe the music and costumes used in the dance?
  • What shapes and movements did the performers use?

Vocabulary: compose, costumes, dance, directions, levels, movement, music, perform, performers, sequence, shape, space.

Making connections through related content

Mathematics:

  • Forming groups: Copy, continue and create patterns
  • Geometric measure: Position: Describe position and movement of oneself
  • Two-dimensional spatial structure: 2D shapes: Sort, describe and name familiar shapes; 2D shapes: Represent shapes

PDHPE:

  • Movement skill and physical activity
  • Self-management and interpersonal skills

Access content points

Access content points support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. The decision for a student to follow access content points should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning. Teachers can use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome.

When teaching access content points, consider that students may respond to and demonstrate learning in a range of ways, including through nonverbal language such as gaze, gesturing, and pointing to or selecting objects, images or words.

When developing movement skills and an understanding of dance, students may:

  • engage in guided dance games using movements in response to a stimulus, such as music speeding up, slowing down, stopping or starting; lights flashing, or images showing start, stop or individual movements
  • match shapes or movements to still images from a dance to identify shapes or movements used
  • use an emotions chart to communicate how the dance made them feel.

Reducing cognitive load and simplifying information or instructions can also assist students with significant intellectual disability to develop movement skills. This can be done by:

  • using one-step or 2-step instructions
  • pairing instructions with visual supports
  • minimising error by first introducing movements that the student is likely to succeed with, then gradually increasing the complexity
  • providing plenty of time for students to demonstrate a movement and multiple opportunities for practice.

When teaching access content points, teachers may see opportunities to use least-to-most prompting (prompts that gradually increase in their level of support for the student). The prompt hierarchy below shows one way that prompts can be ordered in terms of the level of dependence on the prompt. The goal is to increase independence through the choice of prompt and by fading out the prompt as soon as possible.

Image long description: The words ‘Gestural’, ‘Verbal’, ‘Visual’ and ‘Physical’ are placed from left to right along an arrow that points to the right. The far left of the arrow is labelled ‘Least support’, and the far right of the arrow is labelled ‘Most support’.

For example:

  • Gestural: pointing to or indicating the dance space
  • Verbal: prompting a response by asking or rephrasing a question (for example, ‘How did you feel when the dancer moved slowly in the dance?’)
  • Visual: using images of footprints on the ground to indicate where students should place their feet
  • Physical: moving the student’s arm up or down in response to music.

Note: Care should be taken that physical prompting does not limit the student’s freedom of movement. Consent should be gained from the student before engaging in physical prompts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Drama is a practice of embodied storytelling and a form of communication in cultures around the world. Humans have an innate desire to explore the way people interact with one another and the world. Drama experiences widen students’ understandings of people and relationships as they explore situations from different perspectives. Students develop empathy as they experience what it feels like to ‘walk in someone else’s shoes’.

In Early Stage 1, students’ natural desire to play is extended in drama. Students engage in dramatic play, taking on roles and characters and exploring situations by imagining ideas, stories and worlds. As students observe drama from contexts around the world, they begin to recognise the importance of storytelling in all cultures.

Some students with disability may need adjustments to access and participate in dramatic experiences. This could include adjustments to support movement, communication, access to the drama space, sensory experiences and collaboration with others.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development is essential to support student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language and vocabulary of the dramatic elements provides the foundations for learning in the context of drama.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following dramatic elements in Early Stage 1.

Dramatic elementFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Role

Points of view, objects or personas presented through embodiment.		What role would you like to play?

What roles were there in the performance?		Role, person, animal, imaginary creature.
Character

A dramatic role built with complexity, personality and/or background.		How will you show what your character is feeling?

What did you find interesting about the characters in the story?		Character, feelings.
Situation

The circumstances that characters experience and shape through their actions and intentions.		Where is your drama taking place?

How would you describe the story of this drama?		Time, place, situation.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes:

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions; Understanding and using grammar when interacting; Oral narrative
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words
  • Understanding and responding to literature: Narrative; Character

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in Early Stage 1 develops student understanding of how people and animals are represented in Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends.

Making and Performing: Drama is made and performed by embodying and enacting feelings, ideas, roles and situations

Establishing a drama space is important for designating where the action of the drama will take place. This space creates a distinction between performers and the audience. Movement within a space is foundational for developing drama skills. A drama space can be established by:

  • students forming a comfortable circle, either sitting or standing
  • students taking turns to perform in the middle of the circle, with those watching forming the audience
  • using tactile cues on the floor for students who require adjustments (for example, for vision support).

Students engage in dramatic play to enact feelings, ideas, roles and situations by:

  • using dress-up clothes to represent roles and characters (for example, a straw hat for a farmer, an apron for a chef, and a crown for a king or queen)
  • using objects and toys to represent situations (for example, a pile of books for a situation in a library, a toy stethoscope for a situation in a medical centre, or a toy cash register for a situation in a shop)
  • using toys or puppets (for example, bears, dolls, hand puppets or finger puppets that the students speak for when playing).

Vocal exercises that develop awareness of breath and voice are important warm-ups in drama. They prepare students for speaking as a character in dramatic play, such as using a deep voice for a bossy giant or a squeaky voice for a scared mouse.

Students may explore mime and movement by moving around the space as people, animals or imaginary characters while instrumental music is played. Students might imagine being toys in a toy store that have come to life at night, or insects in a garden searching for nectar in a flower. Students can explore miming simple actions with a partner, taking turns to copy the other person’s movements, like looking in a mirror.

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs to peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups to the wider school community.

Appreciating: Drama can be experienced and described

Students make connections with drama in their own lives by identifying the contexts where they have experienced drama including entertainment, celebrations, ceremonies and cultural practices.

Engaging with drama from cultures and contexts around the world provides students with a window for viewing drama from various places. Students may draw from their own experiences to connect with different dramatic works. Students may experience drama through live theatre performances, recordings of live shows or school performances by students.

Students may express their ideas or feelings about a drama experience through oral descriptions, drawings or their preferred communication method, responding to prompts such as:

  • What was your favourite part of the performance?
  • Can you draw a character from the performance?
  • What words would you use to describe the performance?

Access content points

Access content points support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. The decision for a student to follow access content points should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning. Teachers can use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome.

When teaching access content points, consider that students may respond to and demonstrate learning in a range of ways, including through nonverbal language such as eye gaze, gesturing, and pointing to or selecting objects, images or words.

When developing knowledge and skills in drama, students may:

  • enact a character or role using mime or gesture
  • match images of props, clothing or objects with images of characters
  • identify cultural or contextual cues in a performance, such as setting, clothing or tradition, by selecting images or words or using simple sentences
  • use an emotions chart to communicate how a performance made them feel.

When teaching access content points, teachers may see opportunities to use least-to-most prompting (prompts that gradually increase in their level of support for the student). The prompt hierarchy below shows one way that prompts can be ordered in terms of the level of dependence on the prompt. The goal is to increase independence through the choice of prompt and by fading out the prompt as soon as possible.

Image long description: The words ‘Gestural’, ‘Verbal’, ‘Visual’ and ‘Physical’ are placed from left to right along an arrow that points to the right. The far left of the arrow is labelled ‘Least support’, and the far right of the arrow is labelled ‘Most support’.

For example:

  • Gestural: tapping your head to prompt a student to put on a hat to get into character
  • Verbal: prompting a response by asking or rephrasing a question (for example, ‘What else can you tell me about how it made you feel?’)
  • Visual: providing visual supports for instructions for dramatic play
  • Physical: moving the student’s arm up or down as part of the character’s actions.

Note: Care should be taken that physical prompting does not limit the student’s freedom of movement. Consent should be gained from the student before engaging in physical prompts.

content.value:
Why is it important?

Music is a form of personal and cultural expression and a way of connecting through sound and silence. Music has occupied a significant place in cultures around the world and across times. Learning in music stimulates students’ curiosity and creativity, and enables personal expression through sound. Performing, listening and composing music contributes to cognitive development, memory and wellbeing.

Developing aural awareness is foundational to music education, and listening is integral to all musical experiences. Listening skills include the ability to focus on, hear, understand and respond to musical stimuli, and to discriminate between sounds and silence. For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, listening may include the use of assistive technology, or accessing music through touch or sight.

In Early Stage 1, participating in singing, chanting, body percussion and gesturing to engage with rhymes or songs can support students to develop phonological awareness skills that underpin literacy development. Learning about rhythm and beat in music can help students build understanding of the English Early Stage 1 content groups Words and Syllables.

‘Music learning, specifically the act of keeping a steady beat, helps create auditory processing stability in a child’s brain. That stability supports their ability to extend that auditory processing from beat to speech and language. This starts with phonological memory and awareness and helps them play with the structures and forms of words easily.’ (Bonacina et al. 2018)1

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Music provides a rich platform on which to build a musical vocabulary. The elements of music are a good starting point for explicitly teaching vocabulary in the context of music.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require specific and targeted teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following aspects of the elements of music in Early Stage 1.

Element of musicKey questionsVocabulary examples
Duration

The lengths of sounds and silences in music.		How can you show the beat or rhythm by clapping or using body percussion?Sound, silence, beat, rhythm, faster, slower, duration.
Pitch

The relative highness or lowness of sounds.		Which instrument is making the higher or lower sounds?

Higher, lower, repetition, patterns.


Performing media

The instruments/voices/sound sources used in a piece of music.		What sound sources or instruments are being played in this piece of music?

Instrumental, vocal, sound source, percussion, body percussion.


Timbre

The distinctive quality of a sound.		How do you think the sounds are being made?

Effects created by hitting, shaking, scraping, blowing, vocalising.


Dynamics

The volume of sound.		Is this sound louder or softer than the other sound?

Volume, getting louder, getting quieter.


Structure

The design or form in music. It refers to how a composition is constructed in sections or parts.		What are the different sections you notice in this song?

Same or different sections, repetition and patterns.



The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes:

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions; Understanding and using grammar when interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in this focus area supports students to identify how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use a combination of sounds made by instruments, voice and body movements to represent significant Aboriginal Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends.

Performing and composing: Music is performed and made by organising sound through singing, moving and playing

Singing, moving, playing and listening are foundational to music education. They provide many benefits, both musically and holistically, for the learner in the early years of school.

Singing develops vocalisation, intonation, vocabulary, working memory, connectedness and musical competence. Explicitly teach students rhymes and tongue twisters, using memory to repeat words and phrases. Use echo to sing simple melodic patterns and pitch matching. Support students to innovate and improvise on well-known rhymes or songs, changing words or substituting a new word or action. Teachers can also build a wide repertoire of songs through singing games and chants used in assemblies and classroom routines, such as when transitioning between lessons, or as tools to gain students’ attention. Encourage students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing to feel their throat or diaphragm when they sing so they can feel the vibration.

Moving is linked to wellbeing as it relates to self-expression through gesture, speaking, body language, music and dance. In music, moving develops foundational understanding of rhythm, beat and making sounds. All bodies are diverse and move in different ways. Some students with physical disability may require adjustments, including assistive devices.

Provide opportunities for students to use body percussion with action, moving to the beat while singing. Clap patterns and have students repeat them using memory. Create actions to identify sounds and silence in music; for example, waving arms during the sounds and placing fingers on the chin during the silence. Students may respond to louder and softer music changes by moving and using hand, arm or body gestures to show the movement of higher and lower notes. Students use listening skills to move to music at different tempos.

Singing and playing develops aural awareness, motor skills, working memory, creativity and vocabulary. It also supports turn-taking, sharing and social development, and expands the imagination. Arranging students in a semicircle can assist them to follow visual cues and gestures when playing.

Students explore performing by using listening skills to:

  • play a selection of percussion instruments or found sounds such as buckets and pots
  • identify how informal symbols represent sounds and patterns in music
  • use symbols to represent sounds in music.

Image long description: A circle followed by a long rectangle, followed by another circle. The symbols represent a short sound followed by a long sound followed by a short sound.

Image long description: Four scalene triangles, all with a flat base.

Image long description: Three squares: the first with a silhouette of a duck, the second blank and the third with a silhouette of a rain cloud with 3 raindrops below it.

Encourage students to innovate with sound by asking:

  • What makes the sound of a triangle different to the sound of clapping sticks?
  • Can you change the way you play the shakers?
  • Can you use a triangle to suggest a sound for a waterfall, sparkles, a fairy?
  • Can you use a drum to demonstrate the sound of a kangaroo jumping, an emu running, a wombat digging?

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs for peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups for the wider school community.

Listening: Music can be listened to, experienced and described

Awakening students’ awareness of sound will support them to develop active listening and learning habits. It is important to establish expectations for listening behaviours in the class as this will help students to activate their aural awareness. Using the elements of music to scaffold listening experiences will support the development of the auditory processing system.

Provide explicit opportunities for students to identify sounds and the absence of sound. Categorising and identifying sounds supports aural discrimination. Using memory to sequence sounds aurally develops processing skills that support learning. Provide opportunities for students to listen to and engage with a wide range of repertoires and music styles, including vocal and instrumental music from various cultures.

Model ways to communicate about music, using the vocabulary of the elements of music, and provide opportunities for students to describe what they listen to.

Share ideas and feelings by asking:

  • How did this music make you feel?
  • What do you think this music is about?
  • How does this music make you feel like moving?
  • Where could you hear this type of music?
  • Did you like the music? Why or why not?

Vocabulary: chant, duration, dynamics, echo, environmental sounds, metal, mood, pattern, pitch, rhyme, scrape, sections, song, strike, symbol, wood.

Making connections through related content

English K–10:

  • Phonological awareness

Mathematics:

  • Representing whole numbers: Instantly name the number of objects within small collections; Use the counting sequence of ones flexibly
  • Forming groups: Copy, continue and create patterns

PDHPE:

  • Movement skill and physical activity: Participate with others during physical activities

Access content points

Access content points support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. The decision for a student to follow access content points should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning. Teachers can use the access content points on their own or in combination with the content for each outcome.

When teaching access content points, consider that students may respond to and demonstrate learning in a range of ways, including through nonverbal language such as eye gaze, gesturing, and pointing to or selecting objects, images or words.

When developing knowledge and skills in music, students may:

  • demonstrate understanding of pitch by tapping or pointing to the knee to indicate low pitch, the chest for middle pitch and the head for high pitch, when played 3 notes
  • match images or objects, or move the body, to identify changes in music
  • match objects or images of objects to the sounds they make, such as a bell, a ‘walk’ signal at a pedestrian crossing, or a bus or truck reversing
  • match instruments to the sounds they make
  • use an emotions chart to express how the music made them feel.

When teaching access content points, teachers may see opportunities to use least-to-most prompting (prompts that gradually increase in their level of support for the student). The prompt hierarchy below shows one way that prompts can be ordered in terms of the level of dependence on the prompt. The goal is to increase independence through the choice of prompt and by fading out the prompt as soon as possible.

Image long description: The words ‘Gestural’, ‘Verbal’, ‘Visual’ and ‘Physical’ are placed from left to right along an arrow that points to the right. The far left of the arrow is labelled ‘Least support’, and the far right of the arrow is labelled ‘Most support’.

For example:

  • Gestural: indicating the set of instruments to choose from
  • Verbal: prompting a response by asking or rephrasing a question (for example, ‘Now what?’ when a student touches an instrument they have selected)
  • Visual: using visual images to support safety instructions when engaging with musical instruments
  • Physical: placing the student’s hand on the top (batter head) of the drum to feel the vibrations.

Note: Care should be taken that physical prompting does not limit the student’s freedom of movement. Consent should be gained from the student before engaging in physical prompts.

[1] Bonacina S, Krizman J, White-Schwoch T and Kraus N (2018) 'Clapping in time parallels literacy and call upon overlapping neural mechanisms in early readers', Annual of the New York Academy of Sciences, 1423 (1) as cited in Collins A (2020) The music advantage, Allen and Unwin Crows Nest.

content.value:
Why is it important? 

Visual arts have provided a means of communication, creative expression and representation in cultures around the world and throughout history. Learning in Visual Arts develops students’ understanding of the relationships between artists, artworks, the world and audiences. In Visual Arts students explore the ways materials, techniques and processes are used to represent subject matter and ideas in artworks. 

In Early Stage 1, it is important for students to have repeated experiences of making artworks with a wide selection of materials to develop skills and techniques. Students often come to school making marks and images that represent ideas to which they assign meaning. Drawing is a foundation of visual arts and students communicate stories and experiences and represent complex ideas and understandings about the world in their art making. Drawing may include the use of digital software or assistive technologies, including eye gaze technology. Manipulating materials benefits students in developing fine motor skills. 

Supporting language and vocabulary development 

Vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language of visual arts, including the vocabulary of the elements of art and design, provides the foundations for learning. Students develop the vocabulary necessary to reflect on their own artmaking experiences and to describe artworks from a range of contexts.  

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions related to artworks they are making or appreciating see the table below for examples.  

Artworld concepts Key questions Vocabulary examples 
Artist How would you like to begin your artwork? 

Why do you think the artist made this artwork? 		Artist, drawing, make, painting. 
Artwork How did you use the materials and tools to create those effects in your artwork? 

What do you think the shapes in the artwork are about? 		Artwork, collage, colour, dough, line, materials, paint, paintbrush, paper pencil, shape, tools. 
World What is your drawing about? 

What do you think is happening in this artwork? 		Animal, family, friend, person, place, plant. 
Audience What do you like about your artwork? 

What do you find interesting about this artwork? 		Display, share, show. 

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes: 

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions 
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words 

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication forms.  

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities   

Content in this focus area supports students to identify the diverse methods used by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to represent significant Dreaming Stories and Torres Strait Islander Legends through visual arts. 

Making and exhibiting: Artists make artworks using materials and techniques to represent subject matter and ideas 

Subject matter and ideas for art making may develop from students’ own experiences of the world including artworks to represent familiar people, special places, living things or imaginary characters. Subject matter may connect to learning in art appreciation or other learning areas. 

Drawing and painting are foundational experiences for students. They engage with materials to make marks and explore techniques to create various effects. Young students enjoy the experience of painting freely without the constraint of painting within drawn lines. It is important for students to experience colour mixing using paint when making artworks. Students develop an understanding of colour as they mix primary colours (red, yellow and blue) to make secondary colours (orange, green and purple).  

As students explore 3D art forms by making collages or sculptural forms, they experience the artistic potential of different materials and begin to understand the relationships between materials and construction techniques. 

By sharing their artworks with others, students develop an understanding that they can represent subject matter and ideas to audiences. Teachers may prompt students by asking about: 

  • Subject matter: What is your artwork about? What is happening in your artwork? 
  • Artmaking process: What did you do first? What were you thinking as you made each part? 
  • Artistic choices: What do the different shapes represent? How did you use the materials to create those effects? 

Some students may require adjustments to make artworks, including those with low vision or who are blind. This could include using materials with more tactile qualities; for example, natural materials, textiles, hessian, string, bubble wrap, upcycled materials, paints that have added scents to indicate colours, or dough with sand or other textured substances added to create tactile variations. 

Appreciating: Artists make artworks that can be experienced and described by audiences 

It is important for students to observe artworks from different cultural contexts around the world. Students draw a connection between artists and artworks by exploring ways artists use materials and techniques to represent subject matter and ideas. 

Students may observe a collection of artworks related to: 

  • subject matter and ideas (for example, people, animals, places, colour, shapes) 
  • art forms (for example, drawings, paintings, sculptures, photographs) 
  • artworks by recognised artists (for example, Rembrandt, Adélaïde Labille-Guiard, Vincent van Gogh) 
  • art themes (for example, self-portraits, still lifes) 
  • artworks from cultural contexts around the world 
  • learning in other curriculum areas (for example, living things in Science and Technology K–6). 

Students could also investigate self-portraits by recognised artists to describe how the artists have represented themselves in their artworks. 

Title of the image: Self-portrait
Artist: Rembrandt (Rembrandt van Rijn) (Dutch, Leiden 1606–1669 Amsterdam)
Date: 1660
Medium: Oil on canvas
Credit: Bequest of Benjamin Altman, 1913
The Metropolitan Museum of Art

Title of the image: Self-portrait with Two Pupils, Marie Gabrielle Capet (1761–1818) and Marie Marguerite Carraux de Rosemond (1765–1788) 
Artist: Adélaïde Labille-Guiard (French, Paris 1749–1803 Paris) 
Date: 1785 
Medium: Oil on canvas 
Credit: Gift of Julia A. Berwind, 1953
The Metropolitan Museum of Art

Title of the image: Self-portrait with a Straw Hat (obverse: The potato peeler) 
Artist: Vincent van Gogh (Dutch, Zundert 1853–1890 Auvers-sur-Oise) 
Date: 1887 
Medium: Oil on canvas 
Credit: Bequest of Miss Adelaide Milton de Groot (1876-1967), 1967
The Metropolitan Museum of Art

Teachers may prompt students by asking questions such as:

  • What do you observe in the artwork?
  • What is similar about these artworks?
  • How would you describe the clothing the people are wearing?
  • What colours has the artist used in the painting?
  • Does the artwork remind you of anyone you know?

Vocabulary: artist, artwork, black, blue, canvas, clay, collage, colour, dough, drawing, green, line, orange, outline, paint, paintbrush, painting, paper, pattern, pencils, plastic, purple, red, shape, stone, white, wood, yellow.

Making connections through related content

Mathematics:

  • Forming groups: Copy, continue and create patterns
  • Two-dimensional spatial structure: 2D shapes: Sort, describe and name familiar shapes; 2D shapes: Represent shapes

Human Society and its Environment:

  • People are connected to places: People are connected to places and each other

Science and Technology:

  • Observations and questions spark curiosity: Living things have characteristics that help them survive in their environment

Access content points

Access content points support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. The decision for a student to follow access content points should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning. Teachers can use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome.

When teaching access content points, consider that students may respond to and demonstrate learning in a range of ways, including through nonverbal language such as eye gaze, gesturing, and pointing to or selecting objects, images or words.

When developing knowledge and skills in visual arts, students may:

  • represent ideas using simple shapes (for example, a circle for a face, a square for a house)  
  • manipulate pre-prepared materials in creative ways (for example, magazine cut-outs to create a collage, 2D magnetic shapes to create a portrait)
  • identify colours, shapes, symbols or subject matter in an artwork by matching images or words to the artwork
  • find matching pairs of artworks according to subject matter (for example, in a collection of portraits find 2 people wearing a hat, 2 people wearing glasses, 2 pictures of children)
  • use an emotions chart to express their feelings about the artmaking process or to express how an artwork makes them feel.

When teaching access content points, teachers may see opportunities to use least-to-most prompting (prompts that gradually increase in their level of support for the student). The prompt hierarchy below shows one way that prompts can be ordered in terms of the level of dependence on the prompt. The goal is to increase independence through the choice of prompt and by fading out the prompt as soon as possible.

Image long description: The words ‘Gestural’, ‘Verbal’, ‘Visual’ and ‘Physical’ are placed from left to right along an arrow that points to the right. The far left of the arrow is labelled ‘Least support’ and the far right of the arrow is labelled 'Most support'.

For example: 

  • Gestural: pointing to or indicating the materials a student can use to create their artwork
  • Verbal: prompting a response by asking or rephrasing a question (for example, ‘What else could you add to create a feeling of joy in your artwork?’)
  • Visual: providing visual supports for instructions for using art materials and tools
  • Physical: hand-over-hand support to use a paintbrush.

Note: Care should be taken that physical prompting does not limit the student’s freedom of movement. Consent should be gained from the student before engaging in physical prompts.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Dance is a distinct form of movement that is universal to the human experience. Throughout time, dance has brought people together to share knowledge, culture and ideas. In dance, students use the body as an instrument to express and communicate ideas.

In Stage 1, it is important for students to explore ways to communicate ideas through dance shapes and movements. As they explore dance from cultural contexts around the world, they begin to recognise that ideas are conveyed in distinct ways.

As a movement-based artform, dance is beneficial to motor development, strength, and physical and emotional wellbeing. All bodies are diverse and move in different ways. Some students with physical disability may require adjustments, including assistive devices such as walkers or wheelchairs. Adjustments can be made to the environment, equipment and instructions to create an inclusive learning environment.

There are opportunities for connection with PDHPE Movement skill and physical activity content, particularly regarding spatial awareness, static and dynamic balance, side gallop, and participating in physical activities that provide enjoyment and motivation to be physically active.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching the language and vocabulary of the elements of dance – space, time and dynamics – supports students to understand and describe dance as they learn to compose, perform and appreciate it.  

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following elements of dance in Stage 1.

Element of danceFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Space
The components of space including shape, level, direction, dimension, pathways, floor patterns and stage space.		How can you use the space to include movements at different levels?

How will you connect shapes and movements to make a sequence?

How did the dancers use the level, direction or pathway of movement to communicate an idea?

High/medium/low level, left/right direction, straight/irregular pathway.


Time
The components of time, including metre, rhythm, accent, tempo, duration and stillness.		How can you change your movements in response to faster, slower or different sounds?

How did the performers use shapes and movements in response to tempo and rhythm changes in the music?

Stillness, tempo, rhythm, speed of movement.


Dynamics
The release of energy, weight and/or force over a period of time to create movement qualities.		How can you make your movements more gentle or more forceful?

What types of expressive movements did the performers use during the performance?

Bounce, explode, swoop, float, swirl, soft, strong, light, heavy movements.



The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes:

  • Oral language and communication: Social and learning interactions; Understanding and using grammar when interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Stage 1 content provides students with opportunities to gain an understanding of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dances as important Cultural practices. Students will explore movements featured in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander dances.

Composing: Dance is composed to communicate ideas through shapes and movements

Students compose dance by improvising and experimenting with ways to combine shapes and movements into simple sequences. They begin to develop an understanding of how the elements of dance are used to communicate ideas. Students demonstrate communication skills to support cooperation when composing dance with peers.

Stimuli such as music, objects, photographs or texts can be used to inspire students to explore ways to compose body shapes and movements. Teachers can support students by using simple visual prompts such as those below.

Image long description: A series of stick figures demonstrating different body shapes and movements. The first is a pair of figures appear to be crouched slightly or mid-jump The second is standing on one leg with arms wide. In the third, standing upright with arms slightly outstretched. The last figure is standing on one leg, the other stretched out behind it, with one arm reaching up to a star symbol.

Students use their imaginations to explore how they can creatively connect shapes and movements into sequences and move their bodies through space to express ideas. Teachers may use a stimulus or idea that connects to learning in other areas. For example, students may use shapes and movements to represent changes in a plant as it grows, which reflects learning in Science and Technology.

Teachers play an important role in ensuring students develop safe dance practices by engaging in warm-up and cool-down exercises.

Performing: Dance is performed to communicate ideas through shapes and movements

As students begin to develop greater body control, they are able to communicate ideas in more deliberate ways. They cooperate with peers to combine and link shapes and movements into short sequences to perform for an informal audience such as a peer, or a wider audience such as the class or the school.

Teachers may support students to reflect on their own dance making and performing by identifying aspects they think were successful and aspects they would like to improve. Using the elements of dance to reflect on and communicate ideas about dance provides teachers with insights into the vocabulary and understanding that students have developed and are able to use. For example, students may reflect on their use of dynamics, and how energetic, explosive movements or soft, floating movements contributed to the way they communicated ideas.

Appreciating: Ideas are conveyed in various ways in dance

By observing and experiencing dance from cultural and historical contexts around the world, students build an understanding of how shapes, movements and the elements of dance can communicate ideas in various ways. They recognise that dance can be experienced and described by audiences and that their own response may differ from others. Students may draw from their own experiences to connect with different dance works. This could include sharing personal cultural experiences of dance.

When experiencing dance from various settings or cultures, ask students questions such as:

  • What types of shapes or movements did the dancers use?
  • How is this type of dance different to other dances we have experienced?
  • How is dance used in different cultures to express important events, celebrations and stories?

Vocabulary: balance, control, express, improvise, locomotor, non-locomotor, posture, response, rhythm, sequence, tempo.

Making connections through related content

Mathematics:

  • Forming groups A: Count in multiples using rhythmic and skip counting; Use skip counting patterns
  • Non-spatial measure B: Time: Describe duration using units of time

PDHPE:

  • Movement skill and physical activity
  • Self-management and interpersonal skills

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Why is it important?

Drama is a practice of embodied storytelling and a form of communication in cultures around the world. Humans have an innate desire to explore the way people interact with one another and the world. Drama experiences widen students’ understandings of people and relationships as they explore situations from different perspectives. Students develop empathy as they experience what it feels like to ‘walk in someone else’s shoes’.

In Stage 1, it is important for students to improvise while in role to explore ways characters might behave and interact with one another. Improvising and rehearsing build students’ confidence and skills in performing. They recognise that stories and ideas can be enacted in various ways as they explore drama from cultural contexts around the world. 

Some students with disability may need adjustments to access and participate in dramatic experiences. This could include adjustments to support movement, communication, access to the drama space, sensory experiences and collaboration with others.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Language and vocabulary development supports student learning across the primary curriculum and is best taught in context. Explicitly teaching language and vocabulary of the dramatic elements provides the foundations for learning in the context of drama.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require explicit teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers emphasise the following dramatic elements in Stage 1.

Dramatic elementFocus questionsVocabulary examples
Role

Points of view, objects or personas presented through embodiment.		What is your role in this drama?

What was the purpose of each role in the performance?		Actor, costumes, props.
Character

A dramatic role built with complexity, personality and/or background. 		How will you use movement or facial expressions to represent your character?

How would you describe the personalities of the characters in the performance?		Facial expression, movement.
Situation

The circumstances characters experience and that shape their actions and intentions.		What is happening in your drama?

How did the performers combine the events into a story?		Events, story, narrative, real, imagined.
Space

The shape and spatial design of the performance area, and the spatial dynamics and relationships between performers, performance area and audience.		How will you move through the performance space?

How did the performers use furniture and props to show the setting?		Performance space, performer, objects, furniture.
Time

The transformation of the real time of the audience to the imagined time of the performance.		What do you think could happen next in your drama?

How did the actors represent a particular time of day?		Sequence of events, beginning, middle, end.

Language

Ways of expressing and receiving images, ideas, feelings and stories, using spoken, visual, written and/or gestural communication strategies.

How can you use words or language to show how you are feeling in the drama?

How did the characters speak to one another and use language?		Language, words, voice, dialogue.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Social and learning interactions; Understanding and using grammar when interacting; Oral narrative
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words
  • Understanding and responding to literature: Narrative; Character

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Content in this focus area provides students with opportunities to explore ways Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander narratives are represented in dramatic works.

Making: Characters, ideas and stories are embodied and enacted through drama

Teachers can prompt students to develop imaginative ideas by using a stimulus such as:

  • objects and props: an item of clothing, an old phone, a toy, a magic wand, a feather, a shell or puppets
  • sound: a bell or alarm, running water or a crack of thunder
  • texts: picture books, poetry, rhymes, or myths and legends
  • images: postcards, artworks or photographs.

Items of clothing or fashion accessories, such as hats, may be used as a stimulus for students to enact roles and characters.

It is important to exercise sensitivity in selecting dramatic objects. For example, some students may use a walking stick on a regular basis, or a dramatic prop may be the traditional cultural dress for some students. Consider appropriate stimuli to suit students’ needs, such as visual or tactile objects for students with hearing impairment.

As students embody and enact roles and characters, they explore language, facial expressions and movement by experimenting with character voices and variations in the style of language they use. Students can experiment with ways to use movement as they embody characters. For example, yawning and stretching to indicate a tired person, or using slow, big steps to represent an astronaut walking on the moon.

Students explore ways to interact while in role by responding or reacting to others by:

  • acknowledging other characters as they move around a space, such as by waving, nodding their head, or greeting them
  • exploring ways a character moves and interacts with others while music plays. For example, magical characters creating potions, gardeners planting seeds or artists creating a large sculpture
  • improvising while creating a short situation in which 2 characters meet in a place and have a conversation, such as at the park, at the beach or in the forest.

Some EAL/D students may need explicit teaching of nonverbal language appropriate for particular dramatic contexts. For example, different cultures may use different nonverbal language for social greetings. Contexts and situations used in drama require social and cultural background knowledge, and some EAL/D students may need to develop the relevant background knowledge about a place or situation before using it in a dramatic experience.

Performing: Drama is performed to enact characters, ideas and stories

As students engage in improvisation, they develop skills in spontaneously interacting with other characters in a performance. Students may work with a partner or in small groups to develop situations and stories using improvisation, still image, mime, puppetry or storytelling to perform to an audience.

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs to peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups to the wider school community.

Opportunities to reflect on a drama performance enable students to consider ways to refine and improve their performance skills. Using the elements of drama to reflect on and communicate ideas about drama provides teachers with an insight into the vocabulary students have developed and can use in context. Teachers may prompt students by asking:

  • What did you like about your performance and what would you do to improve it?
  • How did characters in the drama you performed communicate their role?
  • If you were to change your role, what impact would it have on the story and the audience?
  • How did your role in the dramatic work change and evolve over the rehearsal and performance period?

Appreciating: Stories and ideas are communicated in drama in various ways

By exploring drama from cultural contexts around the world, students build an understanding of how performers communicate stories and ideas in various ways. It is important for students to experience a range of drama forms and styles. They may draw from their own experiences to connect with different dramatic works. Students may experience drama through live theatre performances, recordings of live shows or performances by other students.

As students experience and describe their ideas and feelings about drama, they recognise that their own opinions may be different to those of others. Students may be prompted with questions such as:

  • How did the performers communicate the main events of the story?
  • What types of movements and language did the actors use to express their feelings?
  • How has drama been used in this cultural context to communicate a story or idea?
  • Whose shoes is this drama asking us to walk in?

Vocabulary: character, costume, devising, dramatic play, facial expression, improvisation, language, mime, movement, performance, prop, setting, situation, space, stimulus, style, time, tone, vocal expression, voice.

Making connections through related content

English:

  • Understanding and responding to literature: Narrative; Character

Why is it important?

Music is a form of personal and cultural expression and a way of connecting through sound and silence. Music has occupied a significant place in cultures around the world and across times. Learning in music stimulates students’ curiosity and creativity, and enables personal expression through sound. Performing, listening and composing music contributes to cognitive development, memory and wellbeing.

Developing aural awareness is foundational to music education, and listening is integral to all musical experiences. Listening skills include the ability to focus on, hear, understand and respond to musical stimuli and discriminate between sounds. For students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing, listening may include the use of assistive technology, or accessing music through touch or sight.

In Stage 1, it is important for students to explore ways musical ideas are communicated through sound. Students develop greater musical awareness by engaging – through performing, listening and composing – with a wide musical repertoire from historical periods and cultural contexts around the world.

Supporting language and vocabulary development

Music provides a rich platform on which to build a musical vocabulary and language comprehension. The elements of music are a good starting point for explicitly teaching vocabulary in the context of music.

Students who are learning English as an additional language or dialect (EAL/D) in all phases of English language learning require specific and targeted teaching of vocabulary in the context of learning in the creative arts. Additional advice can be found in Teaching vocabulary to English language learners K–6.

It is recommended that teachers focus on the following aspects of the elements of music in Stage 1.

Element of musicKey questionsVocabulary examples
Duration

The lengths of sounds and silences in music.		Is this sound longer or shorter than the next sound?Tempo, beat and rhythm patterns, rests.
Pitch

The relative highness or lowness of sounds.		Is this sound higher, lower or at the same pitch as the other sound?Pitch, melody, melodic pattern, melodic shape.
Performing media

The instruments/voices/sound sources used in a piece of music.		What instruments or sound sources are being played in this music?Sound source, voice, percussion, wood/wind/skin/string instrument, environmental sounds.
Timbre

The distinctive quality of a sound.		How would you describe the sounds being made?Rich, bright, warm, smooth.
Dynamics

The volume of sound.		When did the music change to become louder or softer?Dynamics, getting louder, getting softer.
Expression

The musical detail that articulates a style or interpretation of a style.		How did the changes in volume affect the mood of the music?Expression, mood.
Structure

The design or form in music. It refers to how a composition is constructed in sections or parts.		How did the music change from the verse to the chorus?Structure, sections A and B, verse and chorus.

The following English syllabus content supports students to develop language and vocabulary skills for social and learning purposes.

  • Oral language and communication: Listening for understanding; Understanding and using grammar when interacting
  • Vocabulary: Learning and using words

Teachers may need to make adjustments to accommodate students’ preferred communication form(s).

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities

Stage 1 content provides students with opportunities to develop an understanding of diverse sounds and instruments used in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander music. Students gain an understanding of music as an important Cultural Practice.

Performing: Music is performed to communicate musical ideas through sound

Students perform music by singing, moving and playing repertoire or original musical ideas. They may use voice, body percussion, sound sources, instruments and/or digital technologies to play, improvise, organise, manipulate and record sounds. It is important to set up classroom expectations about the care and use of instruments, and to establish routines for when to play instruments and when to hold them still. Arranging students in a semicircle can assist them to follow visual cues and gestures when performing.

Singing is foundational to learning in music. Voice is a personal instrument that is a means of expression. As music is an aural art form, the interaction between voice and the ear, through singing and speech, is important for musical development. Explicitly teach students to sing simple songs and rhymes, and to chant, within a small pitch range. Students may need to practise the pronunciation and articulation of some words. When teaching rhymes and chants, provide opportunities for students to predict and fill in the missing rhyming words. Encourage students who are d/Deaf or hard of hearing to feel their throat or diaphragm when they sing so they can feel the vibration. Use instruments that produce clean sounds when accompanying a singer, and explore digital colour coding to highlight the lyrics when singing.

When students play tuned and untuned instruments they may echo or copy short rhythm patterns, which reinforces understanding of the elements of music.

Performances may be informal, such as performing individually or in pairs for peers, or more formal, such as performing in larger groups for the wider school community.

Listening: Musical ideas are conveyed through sound

It is important to set up expectations for listening behaviours in the class. Listening is integrated in all aspects of learning in music and is fundamental to all performing and composing activities. Students experience music and develop aural awareness using listening skills to consider ways the elements of music are used and to describe sounds using musical vocabulary.

Using body movements to express musical ideas is important for listening. Encourage students to use body movements, march to a beat or respond to a melody. Using props or actions to direct listening can support students to recognise when the music changes; for example, moving ribbons or elastics up and down to show the shape of a melody, or passing a ball to the beat, nodding heads for verse, and tapping toes for chorus. Teachers may support students by asking:

  • How did the music change?
  • What are the sections in this music?
  • Do you notice any repeated patterns in this music?
  • How would you describe the overall mood or atmosphere of this music?

Symbols and graphic notation are a way to represent sounds in music. It is important for students to connect sound to physical or printed symbols. Starting with simple symbols or stick notation builds understanding and lays the foundation for more complex notation as students develop as musicians. Some students may need to be supported to learn about symbols or graphic notation through the use of multisensory tools or props; for example, cups and pop sticks.

Image long description: An example of graphic notation with a stick to represent a whole note, 2 sticks joined at the top to represent 2 half notes, followed by a stick to represent a whole note; for example, taa ti-ti taa.

In Stage 1, HSIE students learn how People use stories, images, objects and sites to understand the ancient past. Teachers may like to deepen students’ understanding of music in historical contexts, including ancient music practices, to recognise how music is influenced by time and place.

Composing: Music is composed to communicate musical ideas through sound

Composing focuses on organising sounds to create music through singing, moving and playing original musical ideas.

Students explore ways to imitate and vary patterns and organise sounds into simple structures. They are encouraged to experiment, change, improvise, share and graphically notate new musical ideas in cooperation with others. Teachers can model ways to compose music with students and support them to experiment with:

  • ways to vary speech chants
  • various stimuli to make music
  • ways to use voice to imitate animals or other sounds
  • creating movements or body percussion to accompany songs
  • creating and using symbols or graphic notation to represent musical ideas.

Image long description: An example of graphic notation using symbols to represent sounds. From left to right, the symbols are 2 wave symbols, 2 apple symbols, a zigzag symbol, 2 wave symbols, 2 apple symbols.

Vocabulary:  blow, compose, echo, gesture, graphic notation, hum, instrumental music, modify, musician, perform, pluck, round, speed, strike, voice, vocal music, whisper, strum, symbol.

Making connections through related content

Mathematics:

  • Forming groups A: Count in multiples using rhythmic and skip counting; Use skip counting patterns; Model and use equal groups of objects to represent multiplication; Recognise and represent division
  • Representing whole numbers A: Use counting sequences of ones with two-digit numbers and beyond; Continue and create number patterns

HSIE:

  • People learn about the past by engaging with stories, images, objects and sites: People use stories, images, objects and sites to understand the ancient past
